MESSAGE_TEXT:
La defensa de la universidad pública volvió a ocupar este miércoles las calles de todo el país en el marco de la Cuarta Marcha Federal Universitaria, una movilización masiva que tuvo su epicentro en Plaza de Mayo pero que también se replicó en distintas ciudades del interior, entre ellas Trenque Lauquen, donde docentes, estudiantes, graduados, nodocentes y vecinos se manifestaron en reclamo de mayor financiamiento para las universidades nacionales.
La protesta estuvo marcada por el rechazo al ajuste presupuestario impulsado por el gobierno de Javier Milei y por el reclamo para que se aplique la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario N° 27.795, aprobada por el Congreso y actualmente judicializada tras el veto presidencial.
En la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, centenares de miles de personas colmaron Plaza de Mayo y sus alrededores en una convocatoria impulsada por el Consejo Interuniversitario Nacional (CIN), gremios docentes y nodocentes, con el respaldo de la CGT y distintos sectores políticos y sociales. La jornada incluyó manifestaciones en Córdoba, Santa Fe, Entre Ríos, Tucumán, Salta, Jujuy, Santa Cruz, Tierra del Fuego, Santiago del Estero y Catamarca, entre otros puntos del país.
Desde el Gobierno nacional ratificaron que no aplicarán la ley de financiamiento y sostuvieron que “la única ley que aplicaremos es la de presupuesto”, según habían expresado horas antes de la movilización la ministra de Capital Humano, Sandra Pettovello, y el secretario de Políticas Universitarias, Alejandro Álvarez. En paralelo, el Ejecutivo oficializó un nuevo recorte de partidas para las universidades por más de 5.300 millones de pesos.
Durante el acto central en Plaza de Mayo se leyó un documento en el que se denunció que el sistema universitario atraviesa un “estado crítico” debido al incumplimiento de la ley de financiamiento y se reclamó a la Corte Suprema que garantice su aplicación. Los organizadores definieron a la universidad pública como “un instrumento de justicia social que produce movilidad social ascendente” y remarcaron el rol de la educación pública en el desarrollo científico y social del país.
La movilización contó además con la participación de dirigentes sindicales, referentes políticos, artistas y representantes de distintos sectores sociales. Entre ellos estuvieron el gobernador bonaerense Axel Kicillof, legisladores nacionales y representantes gremiales docentes y nodocentes.
TRENQUE LAUQUEN TAMBIÉN SALIÓ A LA CALLE
En sintonía con lo ocurrido a nivel nacional, Trenque Lauquen fue escenario de una asamblea universitaria y posterior movilización en defensa de la educación pública, gratuita y de calidad.
La convocatoria reunió a integrantes de la comunidad educativa y vecinos que se concentraron para visibilizar la situación que atraviesan las universidades nacionales y reclamar mejores condiciones para estudiantes, docentes y trabajadores nodocentes.
Durante la asamblea tomaron la palabra Patricio Picco, decano de la Facultad Regional Trenque Lauquen de la UTN; Alejandra Eloy, representante gremial nodocente de APUTN; Gustavo Rinaldi, docente en representación de FAGDUT; y Eduardo Álvarez, estudiante en representación de la FUT.
En las distintas intervenciones se insistió en la necesidad de garantizar el financiamiento del sistema universitario y se advirtió sobre el impacto del ajuste presupuestario en el funcionamiento de las casas de estudio.
Luego de la asamblea, los manifestantes marcharon hasta el acceso de la Ruta Nacional Nº 5, donde hicieron visible el reclamo por mayor presupuesto y reafirmaron el compromiso con una universidad pública “como motor de desarrollo, inclusión y oportunidades”.
“La educación pública nos une, nos forma y construye futuro”, fue una de las consignas que atravesó la jornada local, en línea con el mensaje que se repitió en todo el país: la defensa de la universidad pública como uno de los pilares centrales de la democracia argentina.
TRANSLATED_TEXT:
The defense of public universities once again filled the streets across the country this Wednesday as part of the Fourth Federal University March, a massive mobilization centered in Plaza de Mayo but also replicated in various cities throughout the country, including Trenque Lauquen, where professors, students, graduates, non-teaching staff, and residents demonstrated to demand greater funding for national universities.

The protest was marked by rejection of the budget cuts implemented by the government of Javier Milei and by demands for the application of University Funding Law No. 27,795, approved by Congress and currently being challenged in court following the presidential veto.

In the City of Buenos Aires, hundreds of thousands of people filled Plaza de Mayo and its surrounding areas in a demonstration organized by the National Interuniversity Council (CIN), faculty and non-teaching staff unions, with the support of the CGT (General Confederation of Labor) and various political and social sectors. The day included demonstrations in Córdoba, Santa Fe, Entre Ríos, Tucumán, Salta, Jujuy, Santa Cruz, Tierra del Fuego, Santiago del Estero, and Catamarca, among other locations across the country.

The national government reaffirmed that it will not implement the funding law and maintained that “the only law we will apply is the budget law,” as stated hours before the mobilization by the Minister of Human Capital, Sandra Pettovello, and the Secretary of University Policies, Alejandro Álvarez. Simultaneously, the Executive Branch formalized a new budget cut for universities of more than 5.3 billion pesos.

During the main event in Plaza de Mayo, a document was read denouncing the “critical state” of the university system due to non-compliance with the funding law and demanding that the Supreme Court guarantee its implementation. The organizers defined the public university as “an instrument of social justice that produces upward social mobility” and emphasized the role of public education in the country's scientific and social development.

The mobilization also included the participation of union leaders, political figures, artists, and representatives from various social sectors. Among them were the governor of Buenos Aires Province, Axel Kicillof, national legislators, and representatives of teachers' and non-teaching staff unions.

TRENQUE LAUQUEN ALSO TOOK TO THE STREETS
In line with what was happening at the national level, Trenque Lauquen was the scene of a university assembly and subsequent mobilization in defense of free, quality public education.

The gathering brought together members of the educational community and local residents who came together to highlight the situation facing national universities and demand better conditions for students, teachers, and non-teaching staff.

During the assembly, Patricio Picco, dean of the Trenque Lauquen Regional Faculty of the National Technological University (UTN), addressed the crowd; Alejandra Eloy, a non-teaching staff union representative from APUTN; Gustavo Rinaldi, a faculty member representing FAGDUT; and Eduardo Álvarez, a student representing FUT.

In their various speeches, the need to guarantee funding for the university system was emphasized, and warnings were issued about the impact of budget cuts on the operation of universities.

After the assembly, the demonstrators marched to the access point of National Route 5, where they made their demand for a larger budget visible and reaffirmed their commitment to public universities “as engines of development, inclusion, and opportunity.”

“Public education unites us, shapes us, and builds the future,” was one of the slogans that resonated throughout the local day, echoing the message repeated across the country: the defense of public universities as one of the central pillars of Argentine democracy.

MESSAGE_TEXT:
El conflicto salarial que atraviesa la Policía de Santa Cruz sumó este lunes un nuevo capítulo de tensión luego de que los efectivos autoconvocados rechazaran la última propuesta presentada por el Gobierno de Claudio Vidal y decidieran profundizar las medidas de protesta con un acampe en el predio de la Casa de Gobierno de Río Gallegos.
La decisión fue adoptada tras una nueva reunión del Consejo del Salario que terminó sin acuerdo. Los representantes policiales cuestionaron tanto la oferta económica como la ausencia de funcionarios con capacidad de decisión política dentro de la mesa de negociación.
«Es una tomada de pelo por parte del Gobierno», afirmó Ramón Quipildor, uno de los referentes de los policías autoconvocados, al cuestionar que ni el jefe de Gabinete ni el ministro de Economía participaran del encuentro.
Tras el fracaso de las negociaciones, los manifestantes ingresaron al patio interno de la Casa de Gobierno y montaron nuevas carpas para sostener el reclamo.
Rechazo a la propuesta oficial
La oferta presentada por la administración provincial contemplaba una recomposición salarial escalonada que llevaría el ingreso inicial de los efectivos desde aproximadamente $1.220.000 hasta superar los $1.500.000 hacia el final del esquema propuesto.
Sin embargo, los autoconvocados consideraron insuficiente la propuesta y remarcaron que una parte importante de los incrementos ofrecidos corresponde a sumas no remunerativas.
«Pedimos que un oficial que recién se inicia perciba un salario de $2.200.000. Lo que ofrecen está lejos de cubrir nuestras necesidades y además incorpora montos en negro que no impactan en la jubilación ni alcanzan al personal retirado», señalaron desde el sector.
Los efectivos sostienen que los ingresos actuales resultan insuficientes para afrontar el costo de vida en la provincia y denuncian una pérdida sostenida del poder adquisitivo.
Acampe y nuevas medidas de fuerza
Luego de la reunión, los manifestantes decidieron trasladar parte del reclamo al interior del predio gubernamental, donde instalaron nuevas carpas y anunciaron la continuidad de las protestas. Los voceros policiales aclararon que no se trata de una toma del edificio sino de una permanencia pacífica en un espacio público.
«No estamos ocupando oficinas ni impidiendo el funcionamiento de la Casa de Gobierno. Nuestro reclamo es pacífico y continuará hasta que exista una respuesta concreta», sostuvieron los referentes del movimiento.
Además, adelantaron que se mantendrán las movilizaciones y que las guardias mínimas continuarán funcionando para atender situaciones de emergencia.
Denuncias de presiones y amenazas
El malestar también se profundizó luego de las declaraciones atribuidas al secretario de Trabajo provincial, Javier Aravena, quien habría advertido que no existirían nuevas negociaciones mientras continúen las medidas de protesta.
Según denunciaron los autoconvocados, durante el encuentro se planteó la posibilidad de aplicar descuentos salariales y avanzar con denuncias judiciales contra algunos referentes del movimiento. «Nos quieren condicionar para que levantemos las carpas. En lugar de buscar soluciones, responden con amenazas», cuestionaron desde el sector.
Un conflicto que lleva meses
Si bien el reclamo salarial comenzó formalmente en febrero, la crisis se profundizó a fines de mayo cuando efectivos policiales y agentes penitenciarios instalaron las primeras carpas frente a la Casa de Gobierno para exigir una recomposición salarial.
Durante junio se sucedieron distintas medidas de fuerza, entre ellas acampes, retenciones de servicios y autoacuartelamientos en distintas localidades de la provincia. Las negociaciones realizadas el 10 y el 17 de junio tampoco lograron acercar posiciones y el conflicto continúa escalando.
Expectativa por una nueva negociación
Tras el fracaso de la reunión de este lunes, el Gobierno provincial dispuso un cuarto intermedio hasta el próximo 30 de junio, fecha en la que se intentará retomar las negociaciones.
Sin embargo, desde los sectores autoconvocados advirtieron que mantendrán las medidas de fuerza hasta obtener una propuesta que contemple sus reclamos salariales y la participación de funcionarios con capacidad de decisión.
TRANSLATED_TEXT:
The wage dispute affecting the Santa Cruz police force escalated on Monday after self-organized officers rejected the latest proposal presented by the government of Claudio Vidal and decided to intensify their protests by setting up camp on the grounds of the Government House in Río Gallegos.

The decision was made after another meeting of the Wage Council ended without an agreement. Police representatives criticized both the financial offer and the absence of politically influential officials at the negotiating table.

"It's a slap in the face from the government," stated Ramón Quipildor, one of the leaders of the self-organized police officers, criticizing the fact that neither the Chief of Staff nor the Minister of Economy participated in the meeting.

Following the breakdown of negotiations, the protesters entered the inner courtyard of the Government House and set up new tents to continue their demands. Rejection of the Official Proposal
The offer presented by the provincial administration included a phased salary increase that would raise the starting salary for officers from approximately $1,220,000 to over $1,500,000 by the end of the proposed plan.

However, the self-organized officers considered the proposal insufficient and emphasized that a significant portion of the offered increases consisted of non-salary payments.

"We are asking for a starting salary of $2,200,000 for a newly commissioned officer. What they are offering falls far short of meeting our needs and also includes off-the-books payments that do not affect pensions or benefit retired personnel," the officers stated.

The officers maintain that their current income is insufficient to cope with the cost of living in the province and denounce a sustained loss of purchasing power. Campout and New Measures of Force
After the meeting, the protesters decided to move part of their demands inside the government building, where they set up new tents and announced the continuation of the protests. Police spokespeople clarified that this was not an occupation of the building but rather a peaceful presence in a public space.

"We are not occupying offices or preventing the functioning of the Government House. Our demand is peaceful and will continue until there is a concrete response," the movement's leaders stated.

They also announced that the mobilizations would continue and that minimum staffing levels would remain in place to handle emergency situations.
Reports of Pressure and Threats
The discontent also deepened after statements attributed to the provincial Secretary of Labor, Javier Aravena, who allegedly warned that there would be no new negotiations while the protests continued.

According to the self-organized protesters, the possibility of salary deductions and legal action against some of the movement's leaders was raised during the meeting. “They want to pressure us into taking down the tents. Instead of seeking solutions, they respond with threats,” said a representative from the sector.

A conflict that has lasted for months
Although the wage dispute formally began in February, the crisis deepened at the end of May when police officers and prison guards set up the first tents in front of the Government House to demand a salary increase.
Throughout June, various forms of protest took place, including encampments, work stoppages, and self-imposed lockdowns in different towns across the province. Negotiations held on June 10 and 17 also failed to bridge the gap, and the conflict continues to escalate.

Anticipation for new negotiations
Following the failure of Monday's meeting, the provincial government called for a recess until June 30, when negotiations will attempt to resume.

However, the self-organized groups warned that they will maintain their protests until they receive a proposal that addresses their salary demands and includes the participation of officials with decision-making power.

MESSAGE_TEXT:
IMPHAL: Security forces were deployed to Irawat Bhavan in Imphal as the All Manipur Nupi Marup held a protest rally on Wednesday, demanding the immediate release of six Naga hostages.
The organisation submitted a memorandum to Manipur Governor Ajay Kumar Bhalla regarding the ongoing crisis in the state. The demonstrators carried banners and placards to call for a stop to abductions.
Assistant Secretary, All Manipur Nupi Marup, Ningthoujam Premila, said that the rally aimed to convey the people's issue to leaders.
"Our protest rally is being organised for the submission of a memorandum to the Governor of Manipur regarding the present crisis and various issues affecting the state. Through the rally, we want the leaders to listen to the problems being faced by the people," she told ANI. Meanwhile, a delegation led by Manipur Congress President Keisham Meghachandra Singh on Wednesday met the National Human Rights Commission over issues relating to Manipur.
Singh said, "We visited the National Human Rights Commission today over issues relating to Manipur. We filed a complaint to NHRC on the present issues of Manipur."
Earlier on Monday, the Naga Peoples Union demanded the immediate and safe release of six Naga civilians allegedly abducted on May 13, holding a massive rally in Manipur's Imphal and submitting a memorandum to the state government.
The rally began from Tribal Market at New Checkon and proceeded towards Konung Mamang crossing. However, police personnel blocked the protesters at the crossing point. Later, a team of eight members of the union was allowed to proceed to the Chief Minister's Bungalow to submit a memorandum to the government.
Protesters carried banners and placards with slogans reading, "Immediate and Safe Release of 6 Naga Hostages," "Immediate Intervention by the Government", "Justice and Protection for Innocent Civilians," and "Stop Violence Against Innocent People."
Speaking to reporters, General Secretary of the Naga Peoples Union, Imphal, HB Kowarhring said the rally was being carried out peacefully and in a non-violent manner.
"We are holding this peaceful rally demanding the safe release of our six beloved Naga civilians who were abducted on May 13. We appeal to those responsible to release them without causing any harm," he said. (ANI)

Τρίωρη στάση εργασίας στα επιβατηγά-οχηματαγωγά πλοία που θα βρίσκονται στο λιμάνι της Ραφήνας ανακοίνωσε η Πανελλήνια Ένωση Ναυτών Εμπορικού Ναυτικού.

Διαμαρτυρία για το αγκυροβόλιο
Σύμφωνα με την ΠΕΝΕΝ, η συγκεκριμένη πρακτική έχει ως αποτέλεσμα τον εγκλωβισμό των πληρωμάτων εκτός λιμένα, με την Ένωση να ζητά άμεση λύση στο πρόβλημα.
Η στάση εργασίας αποφασίστηκε ώστε να διευκολυνθεί η συμμετοχή των ναυτεργατών στη συγκέντρωση και πορεία διαμαρτυρίας που έχει προγραμματιστεί για την ίδια ημέρα, στις 8:30 το πρωί, έξω από το επιβατηγό-οχηματαγωγό πλοίο “Αικατερίνη Π”.
Το κάλεσμα της ΠΕΝΕΝ
Στην ανακοίνωσή της, η ΠΕΝΕΝ καλεί τα μέλη της και όλους τους ναυτεργάτες να συμμετάσχουν μαζικά στην κινητοποίηση, ζητώντας να δοθεί άμεσα λύση στο ζήτημα.

Protest over the anchorage

PENEN’s call
In its announcement, PENEN calls on its members and all seafarers to participate en masse in the mobilization, demanding an immediate solution to the issue.
“We call on our members and all Seafarers to participate en masse and together demand that a solution be found here and now to the unacceptable and third-world phenomenon of the ‘exile’ of ships and crews to the unsafe anchorage of Rafina,” the Union states.

MESSAGE_TEXT:
‘Appropriate and proportionate’ policing response in Scarva parade, PSNI says
By Rebecca Black, Press Association
Police in the North have defended a policing operation in Co Down amid a pro-Palestine parade and counter-protest as “appropriate and proportionate”.
Police officers, armoured Land Rovers, riot squad members and water cannons were among resources in place in the village of Scarva on Saturday.
It came as hundreds of protesters, many with Israel and Union flags, were present ahead of the passing-by on Newry towpath of the Great March for Gaza, organised by the Ireland-Palestine Solidarity Campaign (IPSC).
The march set off from Lurgan, Co Armagh, to Newry to represent the 25-mile length of the Gaza Strip aiming to raise money for Palestine Aid Ireland and Children Not Numbers.
The Parades Commission granted permission for the march but placed a number of conditions on it, including that no participant should enter Scarva.
Meanwhile, a group called Scarva Concerned Residents had permission for a demonstration on Scarva Bridge, with conditions including refraining from “provocative behaviour”.
A line of police Land Rovers blocked off the bridge which connects the towpath and the village.
As the march passed along the towpath, protesters on the other side of the canal watched on, including a crowd who gathered at a housing development further down the canal where shouting of insults could be heard.
It came after a similar event last year which saw what police termed as “minor disorder” and four arrests, as well as number of people cautioned.
Events passed off without major incident on Saturday afternoon.
Unionists raised what they termed “significant questions” about the policing operation.
In a statement, the DUP said it is seeking a meeting with the PSNI for answers about the operational decisions that were taken within the village.
“This not only served to increase disruption to residents but many of those on the ground felt did not help reduce anxiety and tensions,” they said.
“Residents and participants deserve clarity on this and other issues including whether evidence was gathered to identify any breaches of the determination issued in relation to the parade, including the presence of a banner with the antisemitic ‘from the river to the sea’ slogan on it.
“The fact that the event passed without major incident is welcome, but it should not prevent a full examination of how matters were handled.”
UUP leader Jon Burrows said he has written to both the Parades Commission and the PSNI requesting meetings to discuss the handling of the day’s events in Scarva, and to seek an update on the investigation into the alleged breaches of the Parades Commission determination.
TUV councillor Keith Ratcliffe questioned the deployment of riot police and dogs, claiming “there was never any point during the day when it looked like there was any prospect of a riot”.
“I will be contacting both the PSNI and the Parades Commission to express my outrage at today’s events, and to demand that this is the last time that Scarva is subjected to the like,” he added.
Meanwhile, Lurgan IPSC said its march was disciplined and well-stewarded.
It said part of the route along Sugar Island Road had been “purposely sprayed with slurry” and attempts were made to intimidate marchers.
“Multiple times along our route, we were accosted by hostile counter-protesters in an attempt to intimidate, with no consideration for the families with young children just wanting to pass through peacefully,” it said.
“Just as during our peaceful protest last year, we were subjected to racist and sectarian abuse, all of which has been recorded.
“Our march was disciplined and well-stewarded, and did not engage while slurs were hurled from the un-notified counter protest in a field outside Scarva.”
The group maintained it had abided by Parades Commission conditions and questioned whether the counter-protest had.
“Again, our focus was solely on coming together collectively to stand up against the greatest atrocity of our generation and the nearly three years of government inaction and complicity in it,” the group said.
“We are proud of all the participants today, we can stand over our actions today and are sorely disappointed to be met with such hate.”
In a statement, the PSNI said: “An appropriate and proportionate policing operation was implemented in Scarva this afternoon to maintain public safety during a notified parade and protest.
“Evidence-gathering was deployed as part of the operation and footage captured will be reviewed in due course.”

MESSAGE_TEXT:
Por: José Medina
Cd. Victoria Tamaulipas.-Más de 20 mil personas permanecen desaparecidas en Tamaulipas, mientras colectivos denuncian la falta de personal forense y antropólogos especializados para la identificación de restos humanos.
Colectivos de madres buscadoras realizaron este fin de semana una manifestación en Ciudad Victoria para exigir avances en la localización de personas desaparecidas y denunciar la falta de respaldo por parte del gobierno federal.
La movilización comenzó este domingo 10 de mayo, alrededor de las 10:00 horas, frente al Palacio de Gobierno de Tamaulipas.
Ahí, familiares de personas desaparecidas colocaron pancartas, fotografías y mensajes dirigidos a las autoridades, reclamando mayor atención ante la crisis de desapariciones que enfrenta el país. Durante la protesta, señalaron que continúan enfrentando omisiones institucionales, lentitud en las investigaciones y escaso acompañamiento oficial en las labores de búsqueda.

MESSAGE_TEXT:
The App Drivers and Couriers Union (ADCU) has formally backed a planned protest against Waymo’s autonomous vehicle rollout in Brent, escalating opposition to driverless vehicle trials in northwest London.
According to TaxiPoint, the union confirmed it will support a joint action organised alongside Brent Greens in Harlesden on Friday 22 May, with members urged to attend the demonstration at the Jubilee Clock on Harlesden High Street from 5pm.
The protest follows mounting criticism of autonomous vehicle testing in the borough after reports emerged earlier this month of a Waymo vehicle entering a live police cordon in Harlesden. Brent Greens have since demanded an immediate suspension of the trial and called for a full safety audit into the incident.
Concerns raised by campaigners extend beyond private hire employment issues. Protest organisers have pointed to fears around additional traffic volumes, empty repositioning journeys by autonomous vehicles and the suitability of driverless systems operating in highly congested areas such as Harlesden High Street.
The ADCU has previously campaigned on issues linked to automation, driver rights and employment protections in the app-based gig economy. Its decision to mobilise members for the Harlesden protest suggests opposition to autonomous vehicle trials may become a wider organising issue within parts of the private hire sector.
Meanwhile, in Atlanta, Georgia, dozens of Waymo robotaxis became trapped in a cul de sac after what the company described as a software “glitch”. Waymo added it took community feedback seriously and have already addressed the anomaly in the “routing behavior.”
A video of the incident can be seen by clicking HERE.
(Picture: Olga Gonzalez)

MESSAGE_TEXT:
Fuel price protests: What Murkomen said
Operators began strike in most towns on May 18.
Matatus, buses, boda bodas and other transport operators largely stayed off the roads in major towns.
Audio By Vocalize
Public transport across Kenya remained heavily disrupted on May 19 as the nationwide matatu strike entered its second day, with operators continuing their protest against sharp fuel price increases.
Matatus, buses, boda bodas and other transport operators largely stayed off the roads in major towns, including Nairobi, Nakuru, Kisumu and Eldoret, leaving thousands of commuters stranded and forcing many to walk long distances or seek costly alternatives.
The industrial action follows failed talks between stakeholders and government representatives aimed at resolving grievances over rising operational costs linked to fuel prices.
Matatu Owners Association (MOA) President Albert Karagacha confirmed that the strike would continue after overnight negotiations collapsed.
“We have not agreed on anything. The government, through the Ministry of Energy, can look for the Sh45 we are losing. We are already servicing loans and still cannot pay for some services. The matatu strike will continue until we get a solution,” he said.
In a separate statement, Karagacha added that operators were incurring heavy losses.
“Today, we have incurred losses of over Sh500 million, and we are willing to continue the strike until fuel prices are reduced,” he said.
The action, backed by the broader Transport Sector Alliance, has also seen calls for fare adjustments of up to 50 per cent to cushion operators against rising costs. Leaders urged members to keep vehicles parked peacefully while condemning any incidents of violence.
Commuters bore the brunt of the disruption, with reports of long walks to workplaces, steep boda boda fares, cancelled school activities in some areas, and delayed business operations.
In Nairobi, major roads including Thika Superhighway, Mombasa Road, Jogoo Road, Waiyaki Way, Juja Road and Ngong Road recorded minimal public transport movement as the strike persisted into its second day, with stakeholders indicating that further negotiations may be necessary as fuel prices remain elevated following the latest EPRA review.
Operators began strike in most towns on May 18.

CAPTION_ENDORSE: Protest blocks entrance to ammonia plant construction site in Topolobampo, Sinaloa, Mexico
MESSAGE_TEXT:
TOPOLOBAMPO, Sinaloa — Tensions escalated in northern Mexico as around 100 activists and residents blocked the entrance to a controversial ammonia plant construction site, preventing thousands of workers from entering. The protest, led by the collective ¡Aquí No! (Not Here!), targets a mega-project being built by the company Gas y Petroquímica de Occidente (GPO) in the Ohuira Bay.
The blockade began at 5:00 a.m. and barred access to all employees, contractors, and vehicles. According to Enrique Ayala, a representative of the collective, protestors have given the federal government and GPO until next Sunday to begin dismantling what they call “monsters of death,” warning they are determined to take the movement to its ultimate consequences.
The action follows a massive weekend march that drew over 6,000 participants from across Mexico to reject the facility. Protesters cite catastrophic ecological and security concerns. Chemist Lindra Valdez warned that cooling the plant’s massive reactors with seawater would increase local water temperatures and devastate the bay’s marine ecosystem. More critically, experts fear that a chemical leak from the projected 2.2 million kilograms of ammonia could travel up to 45 kilometers, endangering three generations of nearby populations.
In response, GPO released a statement condemning the blockade, arguing that it directly violates the right to work for approximately 3,000 operators who rely on the project to sustain their families. The company reiterated its commitment to dialogue and respect for the law, urging demonstrators to express their concerns through established legal and institutional channels.
As the standoff enters its second week, demonstrators remain entrenched in 24-hour camps outside the Topolobampo Port Authority, demanding a total shift toward alternative, sustainable fertilizers.
Source: La Jornada

CAPTION_ENDORSE: Valencian Community, Spain government to meet with representatives of teachers' union to discuss demands
MESSAGE_TEXT:
Las movilizaciones del profesorado no son exclusivas en la Comunitat Valenciana ni contra gobiernos del PP. Recientemente ha habido otros casos y todas han acabado igual, es decir, con un acuerdo de mejora para el conjunto de la educación pública y también de las condiciones de los docentes. Pérez Llorca afirma que están dispuestos a atender las demandas de los docentes aunque todavía no hay propuesta por escrito
Si bien es cierto que en los ocho años del Gobierno del Botánico no se dio una huelga general como la actual, también lo es que se negociaron avances en materia de infraestructuras con el Pla Edificant, de fomento del valenciano o de incremento de profesorado. Quedó pendiente la subida salarial que equiparara a los docentes valencianos, a la cola de España, con la media estatal.
En vistas de que no hay avances en esa línea y que a ese problema se suman otras deficiencias que lastran la enseñanza pública el pleno de los sindicatos (UGT, CCOO, STEPV, ANPE y CSIF) han iniciado una huelga general para forzar al Gobierno valenciano que preside Juan Francisco Pérez Llorca a poner en blanco sobre negro un plan con plazos concretos y dotación presupuestaria. Este jueves tendrá lugar una reunión entre los representantes sindicales y la consellera de Educación, Carmen Ortí, que podría resultar clave para el desenlace del conflicto. El jefe del Consell ha pedido sentido común y ha asegurado que se van a tratar todos las reivindicaciones (mejoras de las infraestructuras, climatización de los centros, descenso de ratios y mejoras salariales).
Los precedentes más recientes en otras comunidades autónomas se dieron en Andalucía, Asturias y Catalunya. En el primer territorio, el presidente del PP, Juanma Moreno Bonilla firmó un gran pacto con el colectivo de profesores en abril de 2022, es decir, meses antes de las elecciones, por el que se aprobó un importante incremento salarial que los docentes llevaban dos décadas reivindicando. El popular obtuvo después mayoría absoluta.
Conforme a las condiciones pactadas, los docentes andaluces quedaron equiparados a la media del Estado, con un incremento retributivo anual de 2.030 euros (145 euros en cada una de las 14 pagas) en el caso del cuerpo de maestros y demás cuerpos del grupo funcionarial A2, y de 2.310 euros (165 euros en cada paga) en el de profesores de enseñanza secundaria y resto de cuerpos docentes, pertenecientes al grupo funcionarial A1. Dicho incremento se aprobó para su aplicación de forma gradual, en septiembre de los tres siguientes cursos académicos, es decir, 2022/23, 2023/24 y 2024/25, con un incremento inicial en la nómina de septiembre de 2022 de 43,50 euros para las nóminas de los funcionarios docentes de grupo A2 y de 49,50 para los de grupo A1. Con ello se cumpliría la promesa realizada en su momento, por las fuerzas políticas de la actual coalición de gobierno autonómica.
Más recientemente, el 2 de julio del pasado año, el Gobierno del Principado de Asturias que preside el socialista Adrián Barbón y los sindicatos docentes firmaron el Pacto Asturias Educa, que recogió el preacuerdo alcanzado un mes antes, el 9 de junio, para poner fin a la huelga indefinida educativa a cambio de mejoras retributivas, de personal y reducción de burocracia, y que comprometió una inversión de 45 millones de euros anuales una vez que esté totalmente desplegado hasta 2028.
La situación de Catalunya es más compleja. Tras una huelga del profesorado, la Generalitat presidida por el también socialista Salvador Illa alcanzó el pasado mes de marzo un acuerdo con CCOO y UGT que ha calificó de “histórico”, aunque sin el aval de los otros tres sindicatos que se sienten a la mesa: Ustec, Professors de Secundària y CGT. Los dos primeros son, además, los que tienen mayor peso en la enseñanza pública.
El pacto con CCOO y UGT incluyó un incremento del complemento salarial autonómico mayor del previsto hasta ahora, del 30%, además de 50 euros por noche para los que vayan de excursiones con pernoctación, una rebaja de ratios hasta los 20 alumnos por aula en Infantil y Primaria y 300 millones más para reforzar el modelo de escuela inclusiva.
Sin embargo, la ausencia de los sindicatos mayoritarios del pacto hizo que el conflicto se cerrara en falso y esta semana arrancó una tercera oleada de huelgas que ha sacado a la calle a miles de docentes y que ha puesto en aprietos al ejecutivo de Illa.
Las organizaciones sindicales reivindican mejoras adicionales a las obtenidas en el primer pacto con CCOO y UGT, principalmente aportar más financiación para sostener un modelo de escuela inclusiva que denuncian que desborda al profesorado. “La inclusión sin recursos es una ilusión, no se puede atender el nivel de diversidad que hay actualmente en las aulas, con todos los planes específicos e individuales, sin más ayuda que la que tenemos”, añadían Mireia y Gil, docentes de Badalona.
En el caso de la Comunitat Valenciana, la falta de liquidez de las maltrechas arcas públicas parece el principal escollo para el Gobierno valenciano, un problema agravado por las continuas rebajas fiscales , en la mayoría de los casos a las rentas altas, aplicadas por el Consell del PP. A ello se suma el rechazo al nuevo modelo de financiación que aportaría 3.699 millones de euros adicionales a la Generalitat Valenciana.
En materia salarial, los sindicatos exigen “una recuperación progresiva del poder adquisitivo”, la revisión anual del IPC y la recuperación de la paga extra o el cobro del verano por parte de aquellos interinos que hayan trabajado un mínimo de 150 días durante el periodo lectivo. También plantean la reducción de la temporalidad, la remuneración de la participación en tribunales de oposiciones o la reducción de la carga lectiva en personas mayores de 55 años.
El Gobierno valenciano alega falta de fondos para Educación pero baja impuestos a los ricos y rechaza los 3.600 millones extra de la financiación
Otras medidas solicitadas que tendrían un impacto para las arcas públicas son la creación de 2.000 nuevos puestos de trabajo, el refuerzo de profesionales que trabajan con alumnado con necesidades específicas y una bajada de ratios. En concreto, estas entidades plantean que Infantil y Primaria tengan aulas de 15 alumnos (10 menos que ahora) y que ESO y Bachillerato cuenten con 20 estudiantes (10 y 5 menos que actualmente). Entre otras medidas, cabe destacar un plan de adecuación climática, la culminación del Pla Edificant o la agilización de la reconstrucción de los centros afectados por la Dana.
TRANSLATED_TEXT:
The teachers' protests are not unique to the Valencian Community, nor are they exclusive to PP governments. There have been other recent cases, all ending the same way: with an agreement to improve public education as a whole and the working conditions of teachers. Pérez Llorca states that they are willing to address the teachers' demands, although there is still no written proposal.
While it is true that during the eight years of the Botànic government there was no general strike like the current one, it is also true that progress was negotiated in infrastructure with the Edificant Plan, in promoting the Valencian language, and in increasing the number of teachers. The salary increase that would bring Valencian teachers, who are at the bottom of the list in Spain, in line with the national average remains pending.

Given the lack of progress on this issue and the fact that this problem is compounded by other shortcomings that are hindering public education, the unions (UGT, CCOO, STEPV, ANPE, and CSIF) have launched a general strike to force the Valencian government, headed by Juan Francisco Pérez Llorca, to put forward a concrete plan with specific deadlines and a budget allocation. A meeting between union representatives and the Minister of Education, Carmen Ortí, will take place this Thursday and could prove crucial to resolving the conflict. The head of the Valencian government has called for common sense and assured that all demands will be addressed (infrastructure improvements, air conditioning in schools, reduced class sizes, and salary increases).

The most recent precedents in other autonomous communities occurred in Andalusia, Asturias, and Catalonia. In the first region, the PP president, Juanma Moreno Bonilla, signed a major agreement with teachers in April 2022, months before the elections, approving a significant salary increase that teachers had been demanding for two decades. The PP subsequently won an absolute majority.

According to the agreed terms, Andalusian teachers' salaries were brought in line with the national average, with an annual pay increase of €2,030 (€145 in each of the 14 payments) for primary school teachers and other teachers in the A2 civil service group, and €2,310 (€165 in each payment) for secondary school teachers and other teachers in the A1 civil service group. This increase was approved for gradual implementation, beginning in September of the next three academic years, namely 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25, with an initial increase in the September 2022 payroll of €43.50 for teachers in group A2 and €49.50 for those in group A1. This fulfills the promise made previously by the political parties of the current regional government coalition.

More recently, on July 2nd of last year, the Government of the Principality of Asturias, presided over by the socialist Adrián Barbón, and the teachers' unions signed the Asturias Educa Pact. This pact incorporated the preliminary agreement reached a month earlier, on June 9th, to end the indefinite teachers' strike in exchange for improved pay, staffing levels, and reduced bureaucracy. It also committed to an investment of 45 million euros annually once fully implemented, continuing until 2028.
The situation in Catalonia is more complex. Following a teachers' strike, the Generalitat, presided over by the socialist Salvador Illa, reached an agreement last March with the CCOO and UGT unions, which it described as "historic," although without the support of the other three unions at the negotiating table: Ustec, Professors de Secundària, and CGT. The first two also have the greatest influence in public education.

The agreement with the CCOO and UGT unions included a larger-than-expected 30% increase in the regional salary supplement, as well as €50 per night for those going on overnight excursions, a reduction in class sizes to 20 students per classroom in preschool and primary school, and an additional €300 million to strengthen the inclusive education model.

However, the absence of the major unions from the agreement meant the conflict was only superficially resolved, and this week a third wave of strikes began, bringing thousands of teachers into the streets and putting the Illa administration in a difficult position.

The unions are demanding additional improvements beyond those obtained in the initial agreement with CCOO and UGT, primarily increased funding to support an inclusive education model that they claim is overwhelming teachers. “Inclusion without resources is an illusion. It’s impossible to address the level of diversity currently present in classrooms, with all the specific and individualized plans, without more support than what we already have,” added Mireia and Gil, teachers from Badalona.

In the case of the Valencian Community, the lack of liquidity in the strained public coffers appears to be the main obstacle for the Valencian Government, a problem exacerbated by the continuous tax cuts, mostly affecting high incomes, implemented by the PP-led regional government. This is compounded by the rejection of the new funding model that would provide an additional 3.699 billion euros to the Valencian Government.

Regarding salaries, the unions are demanding “a gradual recovery of purchasing power,” an annual review of the Consumer Price Index (CPI), and the reinstatement of the summer bonus or payment for those substitute teachers who have worked a minimum of 150 days during the school year. They also propose reducing temporary contracts, providing remuneration for serving on competitive examination boards, and reducing the teaching load for teachers over 55.

The Valencian government cites a lack of funds for Education but lowers taxes for the wealthy and rejects the extra 3.6 billion euros in funding.
Other measures requested that would impact public finances include the creation of 2,000 new jobs, increased support for professionals working with students with special needs, and reduced class sizes. Specifically, these organizations propose that preschool and primary school classrooms have 15 students (10 fewer than currently) and that secondary and high school classrooms have 20 students (10 and 5 fewer, respectively). Among other measures, they highlight a climate adaptation plan, the completion of the Edificant Plan, and the acceleration of the reconstruction of schools affected by the DANA storm.

MESSAGE_TEXT:
Why LGBTQ+ groups are protesting in Mansfield this weekend
MANSFIELD, Mo. — LGBTQ+ advocacy organizations and Pride supporters are expected to gather in Mansfield on Saturday following a dispute over the use of the city's public square for a Pride event.
Heartland Pride, The GLO Center and PROMO Missouri announced plans for a protest beginning at 11 a.m. Saturday, June 6, at Mansfield Town Square, located at 101 W. Commercial St.
The demonstration comes after organizers said Mansfield Pride lost access to the public square, where it had hoped to hold this year's event.
According to Heartland Pride, the issue arose during a May city council meeting when another resident claimed he had previously reserved the square for the same date and that the reservation had been misplaced.
Organizers said the resident also voiced opposition to the Pride event and urged city officials not to allow it.
Heartland Pride and its supporters argue the decision effectively forced the event to relocate and has raised concerns about whether LGBTQ+ residents are being treated fairly in the community.
Organizers said Saturday's gathering will feature several speakers discussing the role Pride events play in providing visibility, support and connection, particularly in rural communities. Following the protest, participants plan to gather at an alternate location.
"We created Mansfield Pride because isolation is a real issue for LGBTQIA+ people in rural communities," Heartland Pride organizer Theresa Nicolosi said in a statement. "Last year, we saw firsthand how much this event meant to people who finally felt seen, welcomed and connected."
PROMO Missouri, a statewide LGBTQ+ advocacy organization, has also launched an online petition supporting Mansfield's LGBTQ+ community and calling for continued visibility and inclusion.
Advertisement
The City of Mansfield has disputed characterizations that any one group was singled out.
In a public statement released June 3, city officials said Mansfield is currently developing a formal reservation policy for public spaces. Until that policy is adopted, the city said it is not allowing any group or organization to reserve public property for exclusive use.
"As our community prepares for these events, the City wishes to clarify our policies regarding the use of public spaces," the statement said.
According to the city, no organization currently has a permit or authorization granting priority access to city-owned spaces, including the town square. The city said the square remains open to all members of the public.
The city also encouraged anyone attending planned gatherings to follow local ordinances regarding public safety, traffic, noise, littering and other public-use regulations. Officials noted that vendors selling merchandise in public areas are required to obtain a business license.
Mansfield officials said they support residents' rights to gather peacefully while emphasizing that city resources are limited and urging participants to conduct themselves in an orderly manner.
The protest is scheduled to run from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. Saturday, June 6.

CAPTION_ENDORSE: Oakland education leaders join others in Sacramento, CA for rally in front of capitol building to urge Governor Newsom and state legislature to provide full funding promised by Proposition 98
MESSAGE_TEXT:
Oakland education leaders joined others from around the state in Sacramento on Thursday for a rally in front of the capitol building to urge the governor and state legislature to provide the full funding promised by Proposition 98.
Prop 98 is a 1988 law that guarantees a minimum level of funding to the state’s public schools and community colleges. The governor’s proposed budget includes delaying $5.6 billion in Prop 98 funding. For Oakland Unified, that amounts to about $27 million, teachers union leaders said.
“I want our Sacramento leaders to understand that our students and educators have withstood years of instability, cuts, school closures, and high turnover,” said Kampala Taiz-Rancifer, the president of the Oakland Education Association, which represents Oakland public school teachers and counselors. “In Oakland, underfunding means high turnover for educators, unstable classrooms, less special education and mental health supports, fewer counselors, and higher class sizes, which puts our students at risk.”
School districts around the state are facing dwindling enrollment and lower revenues, forcing them to issue mass layoff notices and consider closing schools.
This year the Oakland Unified board and interim superintendent Denise Saddler have been working to slash more than $100 million from the 2026-2027 budget, including significant cuts at the district’s central office and layoffs at school sites. The district’s strained finances have come under scrutiny by the Alameda County schools superintendent, Alysse Castro, who last month issued a notice of concern regarding OUSD’s patterns of fickle decision making and lack of a solid plan for fiscal sustainability.
In February, the district settled a two-year contract with the teachers union, two months after agreeing to raises for the district’s support staff, who earned some of the lowest salaries in the district. That contract alone will cost OUSD about $40 million over three years. District leaders have not said how much the new OEA contract will cost, and haven’t explained how they’ll pay for either of them.
Saddler, a former OUSD teacher and principal, joined the rally on Thursday.
“As interim superintendent, I’ve worked hard to prioritize the funding we do have to ensure it is invested in classrooms and students, but there is only so much we can do when promises from the state aren’t kept,” she said. “Our students and educators have endured years of budget cuts, threats of school closures and layoff notices. We need to be able to rely on the funding that taxpayers — and I’m one of them — and voters in this state have committed to investing in our students and schools.”
Other speakers included Jennifer Brouhard and Valarie Bachelor, OUSD’s board president and vice president; Oakland city council president Kevin Jenkins, who read a statement on behalf of Mayor Barbara Lee; and union leaders, school board representatives and district superintendents from Los Angeles and San Diego.
In March, the OUSD board unanimously approved a resolution calling on the governor and state legislature to fully appropriate Prop 98 funds and release the $5.6 billion.
The California School Boards Association sued the state in 2024 for not fully funding Prop 98. Troy Flint, a spokesman for the association, told KQED news that the group is likely to file another suit if the state again delays funding.
In a statement from January, Debra Schade, president of the state association, implored the state to find a different strategy.
“While the budget’s education funding may appear generous at first glance, it relies on one-time funding to inflate per-pupil spending numbers and masks the true costs to school districts and county offices of education,” Schade said. “A different tact is required to provide districts and county offices of education with the funding, support, and flexibility needed to deliver meaningful progress toward closing California’s student achievement gaps.”

MESSAGE_TEXT:
As Springfield City Council considers enacting a pause of 120 days on accepting any new applications for data center projects, a group of about 60 people turned up in front of Plaza Towers to protest artificial intelligence data centers on Tuesday, June 23.
Plaza Towers’ Sunshine Event Center was hosting a Biz417 networking and business development event focused on data centers on Tuesday morning. The panel included Trent Overhue, Plaza Towers owner and developer of a controversial small-scale data center being built near Marshfield.
“(The protest) is just raising awareness and showing solidarity for people who are out here with impending issues, like their properties are being affected now,” said Angie Frantz, of Springfield. “All of us, I feel, are indirectly affected.”
During the rally, residents expressed concerns about the impact of data centers on water and air, noise pollution and energy use. Attendees also shared a wide variety of reasons for being opposed to AI technology.
Springfield has met with one developer who is interested in potentially creating a data center within a planned development on South National Avenue, according to City Manager David Cameron. City Council is expected to vote on the proposed data center moratorium during a special meeting on Monday, June 29.
No definition of ‘data center’ in city code
If City Council approves the moratorium, city staff would use the 120 days to analyze land use compatibility, impacts on electric, water and wastewater infrastructure, and noise and air impacts, in addition to the potential economic impact of data center projects.
Springfield would also begin a series of public meetings to gather community input. Cameron said the city could choose to extend the period of study and community input for longer than 120 days.
“I think this is just adding to the work we’ve already done, because I cannot find a clear definition of ‘data center’ in the city code,” Cameron said. “I think it’s important that that be established and defined, but I also think we ought to, we have to define what we believe is being a good environmental steward of the resources we have.”
The term “data center” is used colloquially to describe developments that vary widely in size, scale, purpose and impact, from traditional data storage facilities (such as the one in Springfield Underground) to sprawling hyper-scale facilities like the 2 million-square foot “AI factory” being built in Independence.
Cameron said part of city staff’s work will include looking at existing planned developments and the compatibility of data centers within the mixed use land type defined in the Forward SGF comprehensive plan.
“If you look at the term ‘mixed use’ and what Forward SGF was discussing, did residents, when creating Forward SGF, understand … that there would be a potential for having a data center or a data processing use in that same area?” Cameron said during the Monday, June 22 City Council meeting.
Staff describe developer’s concept for possible new data center
Cameron said city staff have been discussing data centers for months, but pre-development discussions with a developer “brought to the forefront all the work we have been doing.”
The possible planned development has “multiple facets” and “some of the components” of a data center, Cameron told the Daily Citizen. He did not specify the purpose or scale of the project, adding that it is “like a cousin to a data center.”
In an email, Director of Planning & Development Steve Childers explained that city staff learned about the developer’s concept during a pre-application meeting in June. The developer mentioned a data center being one specific use for the basement floor of a two-story mixed use office proposal, Childers stated.
“The property is in a planned development that allows for ‘data processing services’ which staff does not think is the same as what we (know) as modern day data centers,” Cora Scott, spokesperson for Springfield, stated in an email.
Scott confirmed that the site being considered for the development is at 2900 S. National Ave. The property encompasses about 2.8 acres, including two medical office buildings and 30,876 square feet of commercial space.
A company called NSI A1 LLC acquired the property in March 2025, according to records from the Greene County Assessor’s Office. Documents available on the Missouri Secretary of State’s site indicate the NSA A1 LLC was created in February 2025 and has a principal office address in Harrisonville, Missouri.
‘I won’t see the damage done, but I have an obligation to the young ones’
This spring, the community in Webster County reacted with uproar when developers quietly began construction on a small-scale AI data center. The County Commission retained legal counsel to determine its next steps. There is no planning and zoning commission in Webster County.
“We found out after the ground was broken that there was a data center being built in Marshfield, and there had been no meetings, no transparency at all,” said Cindy White, of Marshfield.
“I’m out here at my age representing for the younger people,” she continued. “I won’t see the damage done, but I have an obligation to the young ones. I don’t want them to ask, ‘Grandma, what did you do?’ and I say, ‘Nothing.'”
White and many of the other people protesting outside Plaza Towers said they were concerned about data centers damaging the environment and water supply. Rex Ybañez, who described himself as a “tenant leader” in Springfield, said he is concerned utility costs would rise in Springfield if a new data center is developed.
“Conditions for working-class people would only get worse with a data center implemented in Springfield,” Ybañez said.
Springfield City Councilmember Brandon Jenson spoke to residents about their concerns during the protest. He stated that he intends to vote “yes” on implementing a moratorium on accepting data center applications.
“I’m just really trying to understand what concerns folks actually have to make sure that the analysis and the report that’s prepared by staff provides responses to those concerns,” Jenson said.

CAPTION_ENDORSE: US Secretary of Interior Burgum says he disagreed with beliefs of Patriot Front group that marched across Capitol Hill on Independence Day but defended their right to do so
MESSAGE_TEXT:
Burgum defends white nationalist group’s right to march on Independence Day, citing First Amendment
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum on Sunday said he disagreed with the beliefs of a white nationalist group that marched through the nation’s capital on Independence Day but defended their right to do so, despite concerns from local residents.
Approximately 400 masked people wearing paraphernalia with the logo of the Patriot Front white supremacist group marched across Capitol Hill on Saturday, chanting “reclaim America” while brandishing the Confederate Flag.
“I think that the certainly what they stand for is nothing that I could possibly agree with, but one of the foundational principles of the United States, which makes democracy messy, is free speech, and there are plenty of things that I see that I might personally find offensive, irreprehensible, but in America, free speech is allowed, and this is by the whole spectrum of things,” Burgum said during an appearance on CNN’s “State of the Union.”
The Patriot Front group broke off from the Vanguard America neo-fascist organization in 2017 after the “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, Va.
Their website says its organizational pillars are grounded in the belief that “Democracy has failed America, and it is necessary to organize outside of conventional electoral politics.”
It also adds that “America has a unique national identity founded in European discovery and settlement.”
Advertisement
Their march across the capital and presence on Washington’s Metro system startled some residents, as reported by WTOP.
However, the Interior secretary said the demonstration was a “rare example” of Independence Day celebrations launched throughout the week where people were “unifying” around the American flag.
Burgum also sidestepped a question about whether he would tell President Trump to condemn the group’s presence in Washington, D.C.
“I mean, there are people that are saying death to Israel and death to America, I mean, this is part of free speech in America,” Burgum told host Dana Bash.
“They can say it, we can object to it, but it is … it is something that comes with free speech in America,” he added.
The Metropolitan Police Department said in a statement to The Hill that it “recognizes the rights of individuals to peacefully express their views and remains committed to maintaining public safety and security for D.C. residents and visitors.”

NEW YORK CITY, NY, UNITED STATES, April 20, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — On the evening of April 24, 2026, the weekly tradition of lighting Shabbat candles will be elevated with renewed purpose — one that reflects solidarity, resilience, and an unbreakable connection to the land and people of Israel.
As thousands of individuals unite at private residences, synagogues, and community centers for Jewish National Fund-USA’s Shabbat for Israel in honor of Israel’s Independence Day, some participants will photograph their Shabbat candles before sundown, in keeping with Shabbat observance, and share those images across social media using the hashtag #shabbatforisrael — illuminating a message that the enduring spirit of Israel and the Jewish people cannot be extinguished.
“Shabbat candles have always symbolized hope, peace, and continuity,” said Shabbat for Israel Co-chair David Peskin. “Through Shabbat for Israel, we are transforming that quiet, sacred moment into a public expression of who we are and what we stand for. Israel has long been a light unto the nations, and through this initiative, we are reflecting that light outward for all to see.”
“It is a reminder that no force can extinguish the brightness of our people or our homeland,” added Shabbat for Israel Co-chair Alyssa Russo. “Join us and help spread the light, one table at a time.”
More than 1,000 hosts and over 12,000 participants across the United States, along with 75 congregations, are taking part in Shabbat for Israel through communal Shabbat dinners. Participation outside the U.S. continues to grow, with communities in Israel, Canada, the UK, the Netherlands, and Latin America joining the global movement.
“Every candle lit carries with it a connection to Israel,” said Shabbat for Israel Co-chair Sara Cannon. “When thousands are shared, that light becomes a powerful expression of unity with the land and its people.”
Registered hosts and guests have access to digital resources, including suggested recipes, Shabbat blessings, Shabbat for Israel FAQs, and recordings of several virtual events. These include a cooking demonstration with Chef Lior Lev Sercarz, Co-founder and Chief Culinary Officer of the Galilee Culinary Institute by JNF, and “At My Shabbat Table with Lisa Edelstein,” featuring the acclaimed actress known for House, Girlfriends’ Guide to Divorce, and The Kominsky Method.
Register for Shabbat for Israel by April 24, 2026, at shabbatforisrael.jnf.org. Take a photo of your Shabbat candles before sundown and share it on social media using the hashtag #shabbatforisrael and tagging @jnfusa.

By Leah Douglas
WASHINGTON, April 27 (Reuters) – “Make America Healthy Again” activists rallied at the U.S. Supreme Court building on Monday against Bayer as the justices heard arguments in the German company’s effort to end thousands of lawsuits that allege its weedkiller Roundup causes cancer.
A couple of hundred MAHA supporters ​cheered and chanted on the sidewalk outside the neoclassical white marble edifice during a rally called “The ‌People vs. Poison,” waving signs with slogans such as “No Immunity for Poison” and “How Much Cancer is Acceptable?”
The name MAHA is a modification of President Donald Trump’s “Make America Great Again” slogan. But speakers at the rally criticized the Trump administration’s support for Bayer in this case as well as the use of pesticides in agriculture.
“You cannot make America healthy again and protect the corporations that are ‌poisoning us,” ​Vani Hari, a MAHA activist and author who spoke at the rally, ⁠told Reuters.
Kelly Ryerson, co-executive director of ⁠the advocacy group American Regeneration and another of the speakers, told Reuters the Trump administration needs to change its approach to pesticides to secure MAHA votes in the November congressional elections.
Trump’s fellow Republicans hope to maintain their slim majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate in the midterms.
“MAHA came to vote, ​many people came to vote for MAHA, because of pesticides, because of the promise that was made that we were going to address the effect of pesticides on the human body,” Ryerson said.
The MAHA movement backs Health ⁠Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a Trump appointee, and has ⁠aligned with some environmental groups and lawmakers.
Among the speakers at the rally were various ​MAHA leaders, members of environmental groups like Friends of the Earth and the Center for Biological Diversity, and lawmakers including ​Democratic Representative Chellie Pingree of Maine and Democratic Senator Cory Booker of New Jersey.
Bayer has ‌appealed a jury verdict in Missouri state court awarding $1.25 million to a man named John Durnell who said he was diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma after years of exposure to glyphosate, the active ingredient in Roundup.
The company is facing tens of thousands of similar lawsuits in both federal and state courts across the country. Glyphosate is among the ⁠most commonly used weedkillers.
‘FARMERS HAVE OTHER OPTIONS’
The Supreme Court appeared divided in the case, with a ruling expected by the end of June.
Paul Clement, the lawyer representing Bayer, argued that a ruling against the company “would open the door for ⁠crippling liability and undermine the interests ‌of farmers who depend on federally registered pesticides for their livelihood.”
While the biggest ⁠U.S. farmer lobby group filed a brief supporting Bayer in the case, some ​small farmer ‌organizations have said agriculture does not need to be dependent on glyphosate.
“Bayer has ​come out, they’ve ⁠made major threats to take away glyphosate, and say that our food system will collapse without them. That’s not true. Farmers have other options,” Angela Huffman, co-founder, president and CEO of Farm Action, told Reuters at the rally.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted this month indicated that most Americans are concerned about pesticide use in food crops and oppose protecting companies from lawsuits when they sell cancer-causing products, even if the company warns about the risk.
(Reporting by Leah Douglas in ​Washington; Editing by Will Dunham)

MESSAGE_TEXT:
Community remembers Nolan Wells and calls for more transparency from investigation at Ocean Springs protest
OCEAN SPRINGS, Miss. (WLOX) — On Saturday, people crowded around the intersection of Government and State streets to call out one name: Nolan Wells.
The protest began about 5 p.m. Large crowds gathered as the Black Hebrew Israelites marched past the intersection and down Government Street before returning to the crowd.
Several hundred people attended the event. Many brought signs and waved flags.
Among them was 19-year-old Nicolas Madison.
“The goal of today’s protest, I feel like, would be just to say his name,” Madison said.
He said that having young people at events like this is vital to inspiring change.
“We are the backbone of our society. So if we as young people are able to get out here and say his name, it can motivate other people who are not as interested in coming out,” Madison said.
But there were plenty of older generations taking to the streets for Wells too.
“For me, this means a whole lot because I have my kids in this community, too,” Ocean Springs resident Jeron Lowery said.
It is a sentiment echoed by Quanta Green and by Biloxi resident Gordon Jackson.
“I’m a mom, I have two sons, so it hit home for me,” Green said.
“Nolan Wells could have easily been my grandson,” Jackson said.
But they didn’t gather just to remember Nolan.
“We’re gonna stand behind the family, and that’s why we’re out here. A lot of times, these stories go unnoticed. Because Nolan Wells is not the only one,” Green said.
It’s something Jackson agrees with.
“There has been a long, long stream, historic stream, of young Black men losing their life under very suspicious circumstances,” he said.
Lowery spoke about his personal connection to Nolan.
“So I knew him personally as a kid before he went out to college,” Lowery said.
Lowery’s daughter played basketball with Wells when they were kids. When he got older, Wells also worked for Lowery at his business, renting water slides and bounce houses.
“It’s hard in this generation to find kids that still say yes, sir, no, sir,” Lowery said. “And when he came to me and wanted to work, he said, you know, ‘my mom and dad told me I gotta get my own money.’ And I said, ‘but when you go out to college, I want you to make good choices and decisions and set you up for a lifetime.’ And he said, ‘Yes, sir.’”
Lowery said the respect Nolan showed said a lot about his home life.
“It says a lot about his parents and it says a lot about him. The things that he did while he was here on Earth, it left a statement in a place in a lot of people’s heart. Life is precious. No matter what color you are,” he said.
Lowery said he also wants to see the truth about the Wells case come out.
“We just didn’t get to the facts of what really happened. That’s really what it’s about. The facts. It’s not about the color of the skin. It’s about sticking to the facts or whatever it is,” he said. “If it’s something that happened as a mistake, then just let’s speak about it. Let’s talk about it.”
Addressing Nolan, Lowery commended the young man for the life he lived.
“I’d just like to say to him and his soul: man, rest in peace. And we always loved it, man. And you did everything you could while you were here. And you did a great job.”

MESSAGE_TEXT:
Eugene 'May Day' rallies demand immigrant rights, UO Latine center
- Marches took place in downtown Eugene and at the University of Oregon for International Workers' Day.
- Protesters supported a boycott of Windmill Farms mushrooms over alleged labor abuses.
- University of Oregon students walked out of class to demand a Latine Cultural Center on campus.
Jordan Rodriguez said May Day is an immigrant story.
“The eight-hour work day, the weekend, the right to work without being killed on the job,” Rodriguez said. “Today, immigrant farm workers are still doing the most physically brutal, most essential labor in this country and they’re still being told to stay quiet, be grateful and not so organized. And when they do, they face retaliation with no legal protection."
Rodriguez spoke at the International Workers - Day Without an Immigrant march in support of Eugene Friends of Farm Workers, encouraging community members to support the Windmill Farms mushrooms boycott. The movement accuses Windmill Mushroom Farm leaders in Sunnyside, Washington, of labor abuses, refusing to recognize the formation of the union formed by its workers and more.
The downtown Eugene march preceded another march at the University of Oregon campus, where students walked out of class to join UO's Anti-ICE Coalition.
Sam Howard, UO sophomore and organizer with Anti-ICE Coalition and Young Democratic Socialists of America, said 900 people had pledged to join the walkout.
"This is a point where we can show that we're not just fighting against the university, we're also building community and building a culture that wants to support each other and have a university that works for us," Howard said.
Toby Cole, a UO transfer student involved in Young Democratic Socialists of America and MEChA, has helped organize two of the UO's most recent coalitions: the Anti-ICE Coalition and the Latine Coalition.
Cole said the effort to establish a Latine Cultural Center dates back years but has drawn more attention as fears around ICE increase and the need becomes more stark. When they transferred to UO, Cole found little support outside of the handful of student Latine-centered groups.
Both coalitions are calling for a Latine Cultural Center with its own building, similar to the Black Cultural Center or Longhouse.
President Karl Scholz and his administration have met with the coalition, but Cole said it hasn't gone well so far.
"We don't want to settle for just a room," Cole said, "We should have had a building years ago. We're the next highest student population on campus outside of white students."
UO Communications provided a statement regarding student’s demands for a Latine Cultural Center.
“President Scholz has tasked his team to lead a task force to assess the feasibility of a Latinx Cultural Center with stakeholder input,” UO stated via email. “Once the final charge is defined, we look forward to bringing together people interested in this important work.”
Student organizer Toby Cole wasn’t satisfied with the idea of a taskforce, saying students had already done the work.
Giovanni Bazan, another Latine Coalition organizer, said the same. He said a similar taskforce was formed seven years ago and all they accomplished was a single study and the establishment of the Latinx Commencement ceremony, which were important, he said, but not enough.
At the downtown march, Lonnie Douglas, a member of Jobs with Justice and the Eugene-Springfield Solidarity Network, said the U.S. was not built by billionaires but by working class people.
“May Day is a reminder of something very simple but something very powerful,” Douglas said. “It’s a reminder we are stronger when we stand together.”

MESSAGE_TEXT:
SUFFOLK, Va. — Members of the community held a press conference to rally against the possibility of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement leasing office space in Suffolk.
ICE is considering leasing about 9,000 square feet of office space at the SIMIS facility off Wilroy Road in Suffolk. According to reporting partners at The Virginian-Pilot, the proposed space would be used for administrative operations. That possibility sparked Thursday’s rally.
"No ICE in Suffolk today, yesterday, and no ICE in Suffolk tomorrow," Brandon Randleman said.
Randleman, an organizer of the rally, addressed the crowd regarding the proposed facility.
"We must come together as black, white, hispanic, and races and say what is happening to other cities in the United States, will not and shall not happen in Suffolk Virginia," Randleman said.
News 3 has reported on ICE protests across the country and in Hampton Roads following increased enforcement by agents.
Thursday's rally in Suffolk also included remarks from local leaders, including City Council Member Leroy Bennett. Bennett said the council has already taken steps by sending letters to warehouse operators in the city asking them not to use their space as ICE detention facilities.
"I have had relationships with people and listened to them regardless of whatever the issue might. But ICE is one that I have really taken more to heart and serious about because the effect that it has on so many people," Bennett said.
The rally also featured school board members, political activists, and community organizations, like the Chamber for Hispanic Progress.
"Our immigrant families depend on all of us they have a voice and they know the system and that we have been integrated to do that work," says Patricia Bracknell, founder and CEO of Chamber for Hispanic Progress a representative for the Chamber for Hispanic Progress said.
The City of Suffolk confirmed no zoning applications or permit requests have been submitted related to the Simis facility. Officials said any required approvals would depend on the specific use.
We have reached out to Simis as well as ICE and am still waiting to hear back.

MESSAGE_TEXT:
Demonstrators chant and hold signs outside U.S. Supreme Court on April 29, 2026, in Washington. (Tom Brenner/Getty Images) (WASHINGTON) — The Supreme Court on Wednesday grappled with whether the Trump administration has the authority to end humanitarian protections for thousands of immigrants without facing judicial review.
While an unrelated ruling about the Voting Rights Act overshadowed the arguments, the court’s conservative majority appeared skeptical of the legal challenge to reverse the cancellation of temporary protected status for thousands of Haitians and Syrians.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that Congress gave the Secretary of Homeland Security unreviewable discretion to manage and end TPS designations, arguing that a legal challenge would result in “judicial micromanagement” of foreign policy.
“Congress balanced the risk there might be some decision that’s erroneous or baseless… that would evade judicial review, against the risk of what we’re living through here, which is judicial micromanagement of the sorts of foreign policy laden in determinations and decisions that are naturally conferred upon the political branches,” Sauer said.
But attorneys representing the Haitians and Syrian Temporary Protected Status holders argued that the Homeland Secretary must follow the “procedural guardrails” set by Congress, which include reviewing country conditions, consulting other government agencies, and providing TPS holders 60 days of notice.
“The bottom line is the secretary can terminate TPS, but he must turn square corners and follow the rules Congress set,” said attorney Ahilan T. Arulantham. “In contrast, as we’ve heard today, the government reads the statute like a blank check today. They want to use it to expel non-citizens, but the power that they seek is a double-edged sword.”
Justice Amy Coney Barrett questioned the significance of the legal challenge, which was described as a “box-checking exercise,” if the Trump administration still canceled the designation as long as they followed the procedural steps.
“If it’s just kind of a box-checking exercise, I mean, why would Congress permit review of the procedural aspect, when really what everybody cares about much more is the substance?” Barrett asked.
“I think it’s because Congress and us too, and the millions of people who live with TPS holders, have some faith in government, and they believe that if there is consultation, the decisions will be better,” Arulanantham said.
Sauer pushed back on those arguments, claiming that the Trump administration fulfilled the procedural requirements by “seeking input” from the State Department, though he claimed that even those basic steps were not necessary.
“If the secretary posted a notice on X saying, ‘I hereby terminate Syria’s TPS program effective tomorrow,’ you would say that there’s no judicial review of that decision,” said Justice Sonia Sotomayor.
“Correct,” Sauer said.
The three liberal justices also pressed Sauer about President Donald Trump’s public and social media comments about Haitian immigrants, suggesting the statements show a “discriminatory purpose” behind the TPS cancellation.
