MESSAGE_TEXT:
La huelga docente en la Comunidad Valenciana entra en su tercera semana sin un acuerdo entre los sindicatos y la Generalitat. El conflicto educativo, que comenzó como una negociación laboral sobre salarios, ratios y condiciones de trabajo, se ha convertido ya en una crisis política para el Gobierno valenciano.
El paro indefinido mantiene la tensión en colegios e institutos, con protestas en la calle, centros afectados y una negociación que sigue sin desbloquearse. La Conselleria de Educación ha pedido a los sindicatos una nueva propuesta, mientras las organizaciones convocantes sostienen que sus reivindicaciones de fondo siguen siendo las mismas desde el inicio del conflicto.
La huelga docente llega a su tercera semana
Tras dos semanas de paros, la huelga educativa sigue sin una salida clara. Según la información publicada, el conflicto ha dejado movilizaciones ante centros educativos y sedes administrativas, así como la dimisión de equipos directivos en más de un centenar de colegios e institutos.
El malestar docente se ha extendido más allá del plano salarial. Las organizaciones sindicales reclaman homologación retributiva progresiva con otras autonomías, reducción de ratios, mejoras organizativas y la retirada de medidas que consideran impuestas de forma unilateral por la Conselleria.
Los sindicatos esperan retomar la negociación
Los sindicatos han previsto presentar una propuesta para intentar desbloquear el conflicto, después de que la consellera de Educación, Carmen Ortí, solicitara un nuevo documento para continuar las conversaciones. La Cadena SER informó de que los docentes esperan retomar la negociación con la Generalitat mientras arranca la tercera semana de huelga indefinida. El punto central sigue siendo si la Generalitat está dispuesta a modificar de forma sustancial su oferta, especialmente en materia salarial, ratios y plantillas.
La propuesta económica, uno de los grandes bloqueos
La Conselleria ha defendido una propuesta con mejoras salariales y medidas educativas, pero los sindicatos la consideran insuficiente. Según la SER, Educación llegó a plantear una subida de 120 euros mensuales desde 2027, después de una oferta inicial inferior, mientras los sindicatos reclaman recuperar poder adquisitivo perdido durante años.
Los medios apuntan además a tensiones internas dentro del Consell: Educación habría intentado buscar margen para mejorar la propuesta, mientras Hacienda aparece como uno de los principales frenos a cualquier avance económico.
La protesta ya no es solo salarial

Delhi-NCR is set to witness a massive three-day transport strike from May 21 to 23, with auto-rickshaws, taxis, e-rickshaws, and app-based cab services expected to remain off the roads. The strike has been announced by transport unions protesting against rising fuel prices, outdated fare structures, and alleged financial losses caused by app-based aggregator companies.
The protest has been jointly called by the All India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC) and the Delhi Chalak Shakti Union, with a large number of drivers and transport operators expected to participate across Delhi-NCR.
Why Are Drivers Going On Strike?
According to union leaders, auto and taxi fares have not been revised for nearly 15 years despite repeated increases in petrol, diesel, and CNG prices. They also claimed that green tax penalties, restrictions on old vehicles, and heavy commissions charged by app-based companies such as Ola and Uber have pushed drivers into financial distress as per Jagran.com.
Union representatives said the current situation has made it increasingly difficult for drivers to manage household expenses and continue operations profitably.
Will It Impact Daily Life? What Are The Alternatives?
The three-day strike is expected to severely impact daily commuters across Delhi-NCR. Auto-rickshaws, taxis, private cabs, and e-rickshaws may remain unavailable in several areas, especially during office rush hours between May 21-23.

Office-goers travelling during morning and evening peak hours are expected to face the maximum inconvenience. A shortage of vehicles may also be witnessed near markets, hospitals, airports, and railway stations.
Here are some alternatives commuters can consider:
- Make maximum use of Metro and DTC bus services, which are expected to operate normally.
- Prefer carpooling with friends, family members, or colleagues.
- Use bikes, scooters, or bicycles for short-distance travel.
- Opt for work-from-home facilities, if possible.
- Purchase Metro passes or DTC season tickets in advance for essential travel.
- Stock up on milk, vegetables, groceries, and essential medicines beforehand.
- For long-distance travel, rely on trains or state transport buses.
Meanwhile, the administration has appealed to the public to avoid unnecessary travel during the three-day strike and make use of available public transport facilities. The Delhi Traffic Police is also making additional arrangements to manage the situation. Union leaders have warned that if the government fails to address their demands, the strike could be extended further in the future.

München: Proteste gegen Spargesetz – Kliniken warnen vor Schließungen
Kliniken und Verdi Bayern schlagen Alarm: Ein geplantes Spargesetz könnte ein Milliardenloch reißen und Schließungen erzwingen. Geplant sind Proteste - und kurze, symbolische Klinikschließungen.
Mit Protesten in mehreren bayerischen Städten wollen Gewerkschaften und Krankenhäuser gegen die von der Bundesregierung geplanten Sparmaßnahmen in der gesetzlichen Krankenversicherung mobil machen.
Verdi plant am Mittwoch Demonstrationen in fünf bayerischen Städten: in Würzburg (15.30 Uhr) und Deggendorf (16.00 Uhr) sowie in München, Nürnberg und Kempten (je 17.00 Uhr). Die Proteste sind Teil von bundesweiten Aktionen.
Am Freitag, wenn die Novelle zum ersten Mal im Bundestag beraten wird, wollen laut Bayerischer Krankenhausgesellschaft (BKG) mehrere Kliniken für kurze Zeit symbolisch schließen. Dabei werden zur Mittagszeit zwei Stunden lang die Haupteingänge geschlossen. Über Nebeneingänge bleiben die Kliniken weiter erreichbar, der Betrieb wird nicht beeinträchtigt. Auch in anderen Bundesländern wie etwa Baden-Württemberg sind derartige Aktionen geplant.
Milliardenloch bei Krankenhäusern befürchtet
Hintergrund der Proteste ist das geplante GKV-Beitragssatzstabilisierungsgesetz von Bundesgesundheitsministerin Nina Warken (CDU). Bislang übernehmen die Krankenkassen Mehrausgaben, die durch Tarifsteigerungen für das Personal entstehen. Diese Regelung soll mit dem vorgeschlagenen Gesetz von Warken abgeschafft werden. Hinzu kommen Einschnitte beim Pflegebudget - wo ohnehin bereits Geld und Personal fehlen.
"Gesundheit ist Daseinsvorsorge und darf nicht kaputtgespart werden", warnte die bayerische Verdi-Landesleiterin Luise Klemens. Verdi und die Krankenhausgesellschaft BKG warnen vor gravierenden Folgen. BKG und Verdi rechnen durch die Maßnahme mit einem Milliardenloch bei der Finanzierung der bayerischen Kliniken.
Warnung vor Schließungen
In der Folge seien Schließungen von Abteilungen und Standorten absehbar. Die Aktion sei "der Auftakt für weitere Proteste, wenn dieses Gesetz so beschlossen wird", sagte BKG-Geschäftsführer Roland Engehausen kürzlich. Die angekündigten Schritte könnten im kommenden Jahr eine Lücke von 1,4 Milliarden Euro in die Haushalte der bayerischen Kliniken reißen, erwartet die BKG.
Die Aktionen stehen unter dem Motto "Solidarisch finanzieren. Sicher versorgen. Sozialstaat verteidigen". Die Gewerkschaft Verdi rief nicht nur die Beschäftigten, sondern auch Versicherte, Patientinnen und Patienten sowie Bürger allgemein zur Teilnahme an den Protesten auf.
Verdi: Beitragsstabilität nicht mit der Brechstange erkaufen
"Die Beitragsstabilität der gesetzlichen Krankenversicherung darf nicht durch Sparpolitik mit der Brechstange erkauft werden", sagte Robert Hinke, Landesfachbereichsleiter für das Gesundheitswesen bei Verdi Bayern. Gerade in einem Flächenland wie Bayern seien Krankenhäuser ein unverzichtbarer Teil der Infrastruktur.
Bundesweit würden den Krankenhäusern im nächsten Jahr rund 5,1 Milliarden Euro entzogen, hieß es. Allein auf die München Klinik entfielen voraussichtlich 32 Millionen Euro, rechnete der Fraktionsvorsitzende der Linken im Stadtrat, Stefan Jagel, vor.
Unterstützung kam von Bayerns Gesundheitsministerin Judith Gerlach (CSU), die anlässlich der Proteste Korrekturen an dem Gesetzentwurf verlangt hatte. Es sei zwar verständlich, dass auch die Krankenhäuser ihren Beitrag zur Konsolidierung der Finanzen der Kassen leisten sollen, sagte sie. "Aber damit darf nicht das wirtschaftliche Aus für zahlreiche Kliniken riskiert werden."

Munich: Protests against austerity law – hospitals warn of closures

Hospitals and the Verdi union in Bavaria are sounding the alarm: A planned austerity law could create a multi-billion euro budget shortfall and force closures. Protests are planned – including short, symbolic hospital closures.

With protests in several Bavarian cities, unions and hospitals intend to mobilize against the federal government's planned austerity measures in statutory health insurance.

Verdi is planning demonstrations on Wednesday in five Bavarian cities: Würzburg (3:30 p.m.) and Deggendorf (4:00 p.m.), as well as Munich, Nuremberg, and Kempten (5:00 p.m. each). The protests are part of nationwide actions.

On Friday, when the amendment is debated in the Bundestag for the first time, several hospitals plan to symbolically close for a short time, according to the Bavarian Hospital Association (BKG). The main entrances will be closed for two hours at midday. The hospitals will remain accessible via secondary entrances, and operations will not be affected. Similar actions are also planned in other federal states, such as Baden-Württemberg.

Billion-Euro Shortfall Feared for Hospitals

The protests stem from the planned statutory health insurance contribution rate stabilization law proposed by Federal Health Minister Nina Warken (CDU). Currently, health insurance funds cover additional expenses resulting from negotiated pay increases for staff. This regulation is to be abolished under Warken's proposed law. Furthermore, cuts are planned for the nursing care budget – where funding and staffing are already scarce.

"Health is a public service and must not be subjected to cost-cutting measures," warned Luise Klemens, head of the Verdi union in Bavaria. Verdi and the Bavarian Hospital Association (BKG) warn of serious consequences. Both the BKG and Verdi anticipate a billion-euro shortfall in the financing of Bavarian hospitals as a result of the measure.

Warning of Closures

The closure of departments and locations is foreseeable. The action is "the prelude to further protests if this law is passed in its current form," said BKG Managing Director Roland Engehausen recently. The Bavarian Hospital Association (BKG) expects the announced measures to create a €1.4 billion shortfall in the budgets of Bavarian hospitals next year.

The protests are being held under the motto "Financing through solidarity. Providing secure care. Defending the welfare state." The Verdi union called on not only employees, but also insured individuals, patients, and the general public to participate in the protests.

Verdi: Contribution stability must not be bought at the cost of drastic austerity measures

"The contribution stability of statutory health insurance must not be bought at the cost of drastic austerity measures," said Robert Hinke, head of the healthcare sector at Verdi Bavaria. Especially in a large, sparsely populated state like Bavaria, hospitals are an indispensable part of the infrastructure.

Nationwide, hospitals will face a shortfall of approximately €5.1 billion next year, it was reported. The Munich Clinic alone is expected to be affected by €32 million, calculated Stefan Jagel, parliamentary group leader of the Left Party in the city council.

Verdi: Contribution stability must not be bought at the cost of drastic austerity measures. Support came from Bavaria's Health Minister Judith Gerlach (CSU), who had demanded revisions to the draft law in response to the protests. While it was understandable that hospitals should also contribute to consolidating the finances of the health insurance funds, she said, "this must not risk the economic demise of numerous hospitals."

MESSAGE_TEXT:
"El ajuste y el abandono se sufren día a día": ATE realizó fuerte reclamo en el Aeropuerto y la localidad de El Calafate
En el marco del paro nacional y provincial, trabajadores realizaron acciones para visibilizar el ajuste y exigir paritarias, mejoras salariales y condiciones laborales dignas.
La Asociación Trabajadores del Estado en Santa Cruz llevó adelante una jornada de protesta en El Calafate, en el marco del paro nacional y provincial, con distintas acciones destinadas a visibilizar sus reclamos.
Desde el gremio informaron que la actividad comenzó con una panfleteada en el ingreso al aeropuerto local, donde denunciaron "el ajuste y el abandono" que atraviesan los trabajadores, tanto por políticas nacionales como provinciales.
Luego, la movilización continuó hacia la Unidad Comunitaria José Formenti, donde expusieron problemáticas vinculadas a las condiciones laborales y cuestionaron la falta de respuestas a las demandas del sector.
Entre los principales reclamos, ATE reiteró la exigencia de apertura urgente de paritarias provinciales, una recomposición salarial acorde al contexto económico y mejoras en las condiciones de trabajo. "No vamos a aceptar más silencio ni desprecio hacia las y los trabajadores", señalaron.
Asimismo, remarcaron que la situación actual no solo impacta en los salarios, sino también en derechos laborales básicos, al advertir sobre la precarización creciente, la falta de actualización de categorías y el escaso reconocimiento de tareas.
Hacia el final de la jornada, los trabajadores se dirigieron a la Municipalidad local, donde reclamaron el reconocimiento del sindicato y denunciaron situaciones de "apriete y amedrentamiento" por parte del Ejecutivo.
En el cierre, los manifestantes ratificaron la continuidad del plan de lucha y dejaron en claro su postura frente al conflicto: "No nos van a callar. No nos van a correr. Vamos a seguir en la calle, organizados y firmes, hasta que se respeten nuestros derechos".
Finalmente, desde ATE sostuvieron que el reclamo forma parte de una pelea más amplia en defensa del empleo público y de condiciones dignas para todos los trabajadores del Estado.

"The austerity measures and neglect are suffered daily": ATE staged a strong protest at the Airport and in the town of El Calafate
As part of the national and provincial strike, workers carried out actions to highlight the austerity measures and demand collective bargaining, salary increases, and decent working conditions.

The State Workers' Association (ATE) in Santa Cruz held a day of protest in El Calafate, as part of the national and provincial strike, with various actions aimed at making their demands visible.

The union reported that the activity began with the distribution of leaflets at the entrance to the local airport, where they denounced "the austerity measures and neglect" that workers are experiencing, due to both national and provincial policies.

The demonstration then continued to the José Formenti Community Center, where they discussed problems related to working conditions and criticized the lack of response to the sector's demands.

Among their main demands, ATE reiterated the urgent need for provincial wage negotiations, a salary increase in line with the economic context, and improvements in working conditions. "We will no longer accept silence or contempt for workers," they stated.

They also emphasized that the current situation not only impacts wages but also basic labor rights, warning of increasing job insecurity, the lack of updated job classifications, and the limited recognition of their work.

Toward the end of the day, the workers marched to the local City Hall, where they demanded recognition of their union and denounced instances of "pressure and intimidation" by the Executive branch.

In closing, the demonstrators reaffirmed their commitment to the ongoing struggle and made their position on the conflict clear: "They will not silence us. They will not drive us away. We will remain in the streets, organized and resolute, until our rights are respected." Finally, ATE maintained that the demand is part of a broader struggle to defend public employment and decent working conditions for all state employees.

Gösterilerin temel özelliklerinden biri, herhangi bir siyasi parti veya lider tarafından yönetilmemesidir. Protestolar esas olarak sosyal ağlar aracılığıyla koordine ediliyor.
Her gün akşam saatlerinde öğrenciler, çevreciler, çeşitli alanlardan uzmanlar ve sıradan vatandaşlar Tiran'daki İskender Bey Meydanı'nda toplanarak Başbakan Edi Rama'nın ofisine doğru yürüyorlar.

-Özel koruma altındaki doğal alanların korunmasının güçlendirilmesi.
Yaşanan olaylar Avrupa Birliği'nin de dikkatini çekti. Avrupa Komisyonu, Arnavutluk'u ekolojik normların ihlalinin ülkenin AB'ye üyelik sürecini olumsuz etkileyebileceği konusunda uyardı.

Protesters believe the government is jeopardizing the country's natural resources and ecological balance for the sake of large investment projects. According to the information provided, one of the projects causing dissatisfaction is a $5 billion investment project by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. The project envisages the construction of tourism facilities on Sazan Island and the Zverneç peninsula. A key feature of the demonstrations is that they are not led by any political party or leader. The protests are primarily coordinated through social networks. Every evening, students, environmentalists, experts from various fields, and ordinary citizens gather in Skanderbeg Square in Tirana and march towards the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama.
The protesters' main demands are:
-The cessation of construction projects on Sazan Island and the Zverneç peninsula;
-The removal of concessions granted to strategic investors;
-Strengthening the protection of specially protected natural areas.
The events have also attracted the attention of the European Union. The European Commission warned Albania that the violation of ecological norms could negatively affect the country's EU membership process.
Despite this, the Albanian government stated that it does not intend to abandon the projects. Official Tirana emphasizes that these investments are of great importance for the development of tourism and the country's economy.

MESSAGE_TEXT:
A 52 días de la mortandad masiva de truchas registrada en Pariahuanca, las comunidades afectadas saldrán a movilizarse. Este jueves, alrededor de 10 mil pobladores marcharán hacia Huancayo para exigir la protección de las cabeceras de cuenca de los ríos Yuracyacu, Shullcas, Tulumayo y Achamayo, que consideran amenazadas por actividades extractivas en la zona.
La movilización es convocada por el Frente de Defensa y Desarrollo de la Región Junín y las comunidades campesinas de Pariahuanca. Los manifestantes buscarán entregar su pedido al Gobierno Regional de Junín y exigir al Ejecutivo y al Congreso medidas que impidan la actividad minera en estas cuatro cuencas, consideradas vitales para el abastecimiento de agua y la actividad agrícola de la región.
«El pedido es único: que no exista ningún tipo de explotación minera en la zona. Por eso solicitaremos la intangibilidad de las cabeceras de cuenca de estos ríos», señaló Augusto Gamarra Sánchez, presidente del Comité de Recursos Hídricos de la cuenca del río Yuracyacu, margen derecha.
Los dirigentes cuestionan que, pese a que pericias de la Policía Nacional detectaron cianuro en muestras recogidas tras la muerte de las truchas, hasta ahora no se haya identificado a ningún responsable. Según los afectados, el desastre dejó pérdidas superiores a los S/ 7 millones, afectó a siete piscigranjas y perjudicó a decenas de familias que viven de la acuicultura y la agricultura.
Gamarra también sostuvo que las autoridades no han atendido los reclamos de la población desde que ocurrió la emergencia.
Buscan proteger cuatro ríos
La principal demanda de los comuneros es que las cabeceras de cuenca de los ríos Yuracyacu, Shullcas, Tulumayo y Achamayo sean protegidas de manera permanente para evitar actividades que puedan poner en riesgo las fuentes de agua.
La preocupación es mayor por el río Shullcas, principal fuente de abastecimiento para Huancayo metropolitano.
«No solo estamos pidiendo por nuestro pueblo, sino también por Huancayo. Por eso creemos que la movilización será multitudinaria», manifestó el dirigente.
La protesta se suma a las gestiones que las comunidades vienen realizando ante distintas entidades del Estado. En ese contexto, la congresista Ruth Luque informó que existe una medida cautelar que prohíbe la construcción de una central hidroeléctrica en el cauce del río Yuracyacu y anunció que participará en la movilización.
Cuestionan a Oro Negro
La minera Oro Negro, que opera en la parte alta de la cuenca, es señalada por las comunidades como responsable de la contaminación. La empresa rechaza estas acusaciones.
Entre los elementos que alimentan los cuestionamientos figura un informe químico-toxicológico de la Policía Nacional que confirmó la presencia de cianuro en muestras de agua y tejidos de las truchas afectadas.
Asimismo, la Dirección Regional de Energía y Minas de Junín informó que una de las inscripciones de la empresa en el Registro Integral de Formalización Minera (Reinfo), correspondiente a la concesión Oro Marudy, se encontraba suspendida cuando ocurrió el desastre.
A ello se suma un informe del Ministerio de Energía y Minas que recomendó la exclusión definitiva de Oro Negro del Reinfo tras denuncias relacionadas con una inspección realizada por fiscalizadores.
Pariahuanca también es reconocida por su producción de palta destinada a mercados de exportación. El alcalde Wilson Quispe advirtió que cualquier afectación a la calidad del agua podría perjudicar esta actividad económica.
«Agua sí, mina no»
Con la consigna «Agua sí, mina no», los comuneros llegarán este jueves a Huancayo en lo que será la movilización más grande realizada desde la mortandad masiva de truchas. La movilización partirá del parque Grau.
Su objetivo es que el Estado adopte medidas para proteger las cabeceras de cuenca de los ríos Yuracyacu, Shullcas, Tulumayo y Achamayo, consideradas fundamentales para el abastecimiento de agua y el sustento de miles de familias de la región.

TRANSLATED_TEXT:
Fifty-two days after the mass die-off of trout in Pariahuanca, the affected communities will mobilize. This Thursday, around 10,000 residents will march to Huancayo to demand protection for the headwaters of the Yuracyacu, Shullcas, Tulumayo, and Achamayo rivers, which they consider threatened by extractive activities in the area.

The mobilization is being organized by the Junín Region Defense and Development Front and the peasant communities of Pariahuanca. The protesters will seek to deliver their demands to the Junín Regional Government and urge the Executive and Congress to take measures to prevent mining activity in these four river basins, considered vital for the region's water supply and agricultural activity.

"The demand is singular: that there be no mining of any kind in the area." “That’s why we will request the inviolability of the headwaters of these rivers,” stated Augusto Gamarra Sánchez, president of the Water Resources Committee for the Yuracyacu River basin, right bank.

The leaders question why, despite the National Police detecting cyanide in samples collected after the trout die-off, no one has been identified as responsible. According to those affected, the disaster caused losses exceeding S/ 7 million, affected seven fish farms, and harmed dozens of families who depend on aquaculture and agriculture.

Gamarra also maintained that the authorities have not addressed the community’s demands since the emergency occurred.

They seek to protect four rivers
The community members’ main demand is that the headwaters of the Yuracyacu, Shullcas, Tulumayo, and Achamayo rivers be permanently protected to prevent activities that could endanger the water sources.

The greatest concern is for the Shullcas River, the main source of water for metropolitan Huancayo.

"We are not only asking for our own people, but also for Huancayo. That's why we believe the mobilization will be massive," the leader stated.

The protest adds to the efforts the communities have been making with various state entities. In this context, Congresswoman Ruth Luque reported that there is a precautionary measure prohibiting the construction of a hydroelectric plant on the Yuracyacu River and announced that she will participate in the mobilization.
Oro Negro is being questioned
The Oro Negro mining company, which operates in the upper part of the basin, is being blamed by the communities for the pollution. The company rejects these accusations.

Among the elements fueling the questioning is a chemical-toxicological report from the National Police that confirmed the presence of cyanide in water samples and tissue samples from the affected trout.

Likewise, the Junín Regional Directorate of Energy and Mines reported that one of the company's registrations in the Comprehensive Registry of Mining Formalization (REINFO), corresponding to the Oro Marudy concession, was suspended when the disaster occurred.

In addition, a report from the Ministry of Energy and Mines recommended the definitive exclusion of Oro Negro from REINFO following complaints related to an inspection carried out by inspectors.
Pariahuanca is also known for its avocado production destined for export markets. Mayor Wilson Quispe warned that any impact on water quality could harm this economic activity.

"Water yes, mine no"
With the slogan "Water yes, mine no," community members will arrive in Huancayo this Thursday in what will be the largest mobilization since the mass die-off of trout. The march will depart from Grau Park.

Their goal is for the government to take measures to protect the headwaters of the Yuracyacu, Shullcas, Tulumayo, and Achamayo rivers, considered essential for water supply and the livelihoods of thousands of families in the region.

MESSAGE_TEXT:
Verdi ruft Telekom-Beschäftigte in Saarbrücken erneut zum Streik auf
Die Gewerkschaft Verdi setzt heute die Warnstreiks bei den Telekom-Beschäftigten fort. Erneut sind auch die Beschäftigen in Saarbrücken zum Streik aufgerufen. Vor rund einer Woche war dort zuletzt gestreikt worden.
Vor der nächsten Verhandlungsrunde, die am 11. Mai beginnt, hat Verdi erneut die Telekom-Beschäftigten zum Streik aufgerufen. Davon betroffen sind wieder Beschäftigte in Saarbrücken, Kaiserslautern, Trier, Neustadt, Ludwigshafen, Koblenz, Bad Kreuznach und Mainz.
Darüber hinaus ruft Verdi auch Beschäftigte in T-Shops sowie bei T-Systems zu Solidaritätsstreiks auf, sodass die Warnstreiks über diese acht Hauptstandorte hinausreichen. Es könne etwa zu Verzögerungen im technischen Kundenservice und zu Absagen bei Terminen kommen.
Der Standort Saarbrücken ist unter anderem zuständig für den Telefon-Service, den Außendienst bei Störungen sowie den Glasfaserausbau und -service.
Verdi fordert 6,6 Prozent mehr Lohn für Telekom-Beschäftigte
Mit dem Streik will Verdi nach eigenen Angaben den Druck auf die Arbeitgeber vor der dritten Tarifverhandlungsrunde erhöhen. Bisher hatte die Telekom kein Angebot vorgelegt.
Verdi verlangt unter anderem 6,6 Prozent mehr Lohn bei einer Laufzeit des Tarifvertrags von einem Jahr. Eine weitere Forderung: Gewerkschaftsmitglieder sollen einen jährlichen Bonus in Höhe von 660 Euro erhalten.

Verdi calls on Telekom employees in Saarbrücken to strike again
The Verdi union is continuing its warning strikes among Telekom employees today. Employees in Saarbrücken have once again been called to strike. The last strike there took place about a week ago.

Ahead of the next round of negotiations, which begins on May 11, Verdi has again called on Telekom employees to strike. This will again affect employees in Saarbrücken, Kaiserslautern, Trier, Neustadt, Ludwigshafen, Koblenz, Bad Kreuznach, and Mainz.

In addition, Verdi is also calling on employees in T-Shops and T-Systems to participate in solidarity strikes, meaning the warning strikes will extend beyond these eight main locations. Delays in technical customer service and appointment cancellations are possible.

The Saarbrücken location is responsible for, among other things, telephone service, field service for malfunctions, and fiber optic expansion and maintenance.

With the strike, Verdi aims to increase pressure on employers ahead of the third round of collective bargaining. Telekom has not yet submitted an offer.

MESSAGE_TEXT:
PALMA 23 May. (EUROPA PRESS) -
Trabajadoras de las grandes cadenas de comercios de textil y calzado han secundado en Palma la huelga estatal convocada por UGT contra el convenio colectivo estatal acordado al entender que supondrá un recorte de derechos recogido por la normativa laboral de Baleares.
Este y el resto de paros convocados por toda España han perseguido el objetivo de evitar que los grandes comercios puedan desligarse de los convenios autonómicos y regionales al aplicar las condiciones laborales que recogerá el futuro convenio colectivo del que han firmado un preacuerdo la Asociación Retail Textil España (ARTE) y los sindicatos Fetico y CCOO.
Varias decenas de personas se han concentrado la mañana de este sábado en el Passeig del Born portando una gran pancarta en la que se podía leer el lema 'Convenio de ARTE no. Ni un derecho menos', según ha publicado UGT Baleares en su cuenta de la red social X.
También han lucido carteles que rezaban mensajes como 'El ARTE de robarte', 'No trabajo por amor al ARTE', 'La plantilla no está de reabajas' o 'El ARTE de mangonearte'.
A la huelga estaban convocados no solo los trabajadores de grandes marcas como Inditex, Primark, H&M, Mango o Tendam sino también aquellos de comercios de moda que cumplan las condiciones para sumarse al convenio estatal.
TRANSLATED_TEXT:
PALMA, May 23 (EUROPA PRESS) - Workers from major clothing and footwear chains in Palma joined the nationwide strike called by the UGT union against the agreed-upon national collective bargaining agreement, arguing that it will reduce rights protected by Balearic labor law.

This and other strikes called throughout Spain aimed to prevent large retailers from disregarding regional and local agreements by implementing the working conditions of the future collective bargaining agreement, for which the Spanish Textile Retail Association (ARTE) and the unions Fetico and CCOO have signed a preliminary agreement.

Several dozen people gathered this Saturday morning on the Passeig del Born, carrying a large banner with the slogan "No to the ARTE agreement." "Not one right less," as UGT Baleares posted on its social media account.
They also displayed signs with messages such as "The ART of robbing you," "I don't work for the love of ART," "The staff isn't on sale," and "The ART of manipulating you."
The strike was called not only by workers from major brands like Inditex, Primark, H&M, Mango, and Tendam, but also by those in fashion stores that meet the requirements to join the national collective bargaining agreement.

La disputa entre la empresa Cascia Gases y el Sindicato Químico Pilar continúa sin avances. Mientras se desarrollan audiencias en el Ministerio de Trabajo, el gremio sostiene la protesta frente a la planta del Parque Industrial.
El conflicto entre la empresa Cascia Gases y el Sindicato Químico Pilar continúa sin encontrar una salida y suma nuevos capítulos. Mientras avanzan las audiencias en el Ministerio de Trabajo, el gremio mantiene el acampe frente a la planta ubicada en el Parque Industrial de Pilar y denuncia la falta de voluntad de la empresa para abrir una instancia de diálogo que permita destrabar la situación.
La protesta se sostiene desde hace varios días en reclamo por la reincorporación de trabajadores despedidos y en rechazo a lo que el sindicato considera prácticas antisindicales. Desde la organización aseguraron que las medidas continuarán de manera pacífica hasta obtener respuestas por parte de la firma.
En una entrevista con el programa El Diario del Sábado, que se emite por FM Los Cardales, el secretario general del Sindicato Químico, Sergio González, explicó que el acampe es una de las pocas herramientas de protesta con las que cuentan los trabajadores.
"La verdad que debe ser de muy mal gusto para la empresa, pero son las pocas herramientas que tenemos. Nuestras manifestaciones son pacíficas. Nosotros sabemos trabajar, no es lo que más nos gusta hacer, pero si nos buscan, nos van a encontrar y también sabemos defender a los trabajadores", expresó.
El dirigente cuestionó además la decisión de la empresa de despedir a empleados con larga trayectoria dentro de la firma y puso el foco en la experiencia que requiere la actividad.
"Despidieron compañeros con 25 años de antigüedad e inventaron causas que no existen. Formar un trabajador calificado lleva meses de capacitación y muchos años de experiencia. Eso no se reemplaza de un día para otro", afirmó.
Según González, la situación no solo afecta a los trabajadores desvinculados, sino también al funcionamiento de una actividad que requiere personal altamente especializado.
Denuncias por prácticas antisindicales
Durante la entrevista, el titular del sindicato también denunció que algunos empleados despedidos habrían recibido propuestas para presentar su renuncia a cambio del cobro de una indemnización, una modalidad que consideró incompatible con la legislación laboral vigente.
"Eso es una práctica desleal y totalmente antisindical. Estamos volviendo muchos años atrás con este tipo de conductas", sostuvo.
El conflicto tuvo un primer capítulo cuando el Ministerio de Trabajo dictó la conciliación obligatoria, medida que permitió la reincorporación transitoria de los trabajadores afectados. Sin embargo, una vez vencido ese período, los despidos volvieron a hacerse efectivos.
Desde entonces, el sindicato participa de las audiencias convocadas por la cartera laboral, aunque denuncia que la empresa continúa sin mostrar predisposición para alcanzar un entendimiento.
González también cuestionó el modelo laboral que, según indicó, Cascia pretende implementar en su planta de Pilar.
"No tenemos ningún problema en que la empresa crezca, pero queremos que ese crecimiento vaya acompañado de trabajo digno, salarios justos y respeto por los derechos laborales", manifestó.
En ese sentido, aseguró que la firma busca trasladar desde su planta de Tucumán un esquema de menores salarios, algo que el gremio rechaza de plano.
Hacia el final de la entrevista, el dirigente llamó a fortalecer la unidad del movimiento obrero para enfrentar conflictos de este tipo.
"Es momento de dejar de lado las diferencias y trabajar colectivamente. Cuando despiden a un trabajador, nos están poniendo a prueba a todos. La unidad del sindicalismo será fundamental para defender los derechos conquistados", concluyó.
Mientras las negociaciones permanecen estancadas y no se registran avances en las audiencias realizadas en el Ministerio de Trabajo, el Sindicato Químico Pilar ratificó que mantendrá el acampe frente a la planta de Cascia Gases y las medidas de protesta hasta que la empresa acepte abrir una mesa de diálogo para buscar una solución al conflicto.
TRANSLATED_TEXT:
The conflict at Cascia continues: the Chemical Workers Union maintains its encampment and denounces the lack of dialogue.
The dispute between Cascia Gases and the Pilar Chemical Workers Union remains unresolved. While hearings are underway at the Ministry of Labor, the union continues its protest in front of the plant in the Industrial Park.
The conflict between Cascia Gases and the Pilar Chemical Workers Union continues without a solution and has taken new turns. While the hearings at the Ministry of Labor are ongoing, the union maintains its encampment in front of the plant located in the Pilar Industrial Park and denounces the company's unwillingness to engage in dialogue to resolve the situation.

The protest has been ongoing for several days, demanding the reinstatement of dismissed workers and rejecting what the union considers anti-union practices. The organization has stated that the actions will continue peacefully until they receive a response from the company. In an interview with the program "El Diario del Sábado," broadcast on FM Los Cardales, the general secretary of the Chemical Workers Union, Sergio González, explained that the encampment is one of the few protest tools available to the workers.

"It must be in very bad taste for the company, but it's one of the few tools we have. Our demonstrations are peaceful. We know how to work; it's not what we like to do most, but if they come looking for trouble, they'll find it, and we also know how to defend the workers," he stated.

The union leader also questioned the company's decision to lay off long-serving employees and emphasized the experience required for the job.

"They fired colleagues with 25 years of seniority and invented reasons that don't exist. Developing a skilled worker takes months of training and many years of experience. That can't be replaced overnight," he affirmed.

According to González, the situation not only affects the laid-off workers but also the operation of an industry that requires highly specialized personnel. Complaints about anti-union practices
During the interview, the union leader also denounced that some dismissed employees had received offers to resign in exchange for severance pay, a practice he considered incompatible with current labor laws.

"That's an unfair and completely anti-union practice. We're going back many years with this type of behavior," he stated.

The conflict began when the Ministry of Labor mandated compulsory conciliation, a measure that allowed for the temporary reinstatement of the affected workers. However, once that period expired, the dismissals were reinstated.

Since then, the union has participated in the hearings convened by the Ministry of Labor, although it reports that the company continues to show no willingness to reach an agreement.
González also questioned the labor model that, according to him, Cascia intends to implement at its Pilar plant.

"We have no problem with the company growing, but we want that growth to be accompanied by decent work, fair wages, and respect for labor rights," he stated.

In that regard, he asserted that the company is seeking to implement a lower-wage system from its Tucumán plant, something the union flatly rejects.

Toward the end of the interview, the union leader called for strengthening the unity of the labor movement to confront conflicts of this kind.

"It's time to put aside our differences and work collectively. When a worker is fired, we are all being tested. Union unity will be fundamental to defending the rights we have won," he concluded.

While negotiations remain stalled and no progress has been made in the hearings held at the Ministry of Labor, the Pilar Chemical Workers Union reaffirmed that it will maintain its encampment in front of the Cascia Gases plant and its protest measures until the company agrees to open a dialogue to find a solution to the conflict.

Opnieuw aanhoudingen bij protest tegen noodopvang in Apeldoorn
APELDOORN (ANP) – De politie heeft woensdagavond in Apeldoorn vijf mensen aangehouden bij een demonstratie tegen noodopvang voor asielzoekers. Op de rotonde in de wijk De Maten is de afgelopen tijd vaker geprotesteerd tegen de opvangplannen van de Gelderse gemeente.
De verdachten in de leeftijd van 16 tot 37 jaar komen allemaal uit Apeldoorn, zegt een woordvoerster van de politie. Twee van hen staken vuurwerk af en de derde een rookbom. De vierde verdachte voldeed niet aan een vordering van de politie en de vijfde overtrad zijn gebiedsverbod.

ANP
TRANSLATED_TEXT:
More arrests at protest against emergency shelter in Apeldoorn

APELDOORN (ANP) – The police arrested five people in Apeldoorn on Wednesday evening during a demonstration against emergency shelter for asylum seekers. Protests against the Gelderland municipality's accommodation plans have taken place frequently recently at the roundabout in the De Maten district.

The suspects, aged 16 to 37, are all from Apeldoorn, a police spokeswoman said. Two of them set off fireworks and the third a smoke bomb. The fourth suspect failed to comply with a police order and the fifth violated his restraining order.

Since Friday, the police have arrested people every evening during demonstrations against the shelter. On Saturday evening, the situation escalated significantly. Protesters pelted the police with fireworks, obstructed traffic, and attacked a vehicle, among other things.

Thousands of union activists rally in Winnipeg to protect Canadian workers and jobs
Posted May 14, 2026 4:09 pm.
Hundreds of labour delegates took to the streets in Winnipeg, calling for stronger protections for workers and Canadian jobs.
“It’s important to fight for workers’ rights. Keeping our healthcare the way it is, no longer two-tiered healthcare,” said Karen Schmid, the president of Health Science Association Saskatchewan.
Sean O’Reilly, the president of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, added, “This is the key thing that the workers are there for everyone to help all Canadians from across this country from coast to coast to coast, and we want to show that we want to work hard and we want to make sure our employers are respecting us.”
The rally brought together union members from across Canada who walked through downtown from the RBC Convention Centre to the Union Centre. This is the first time in 40 years that the Canadian Labour Congress held its annual convention in Winnipeg.
“We’re all here standing about, talking about unions and the power behind unions and the importance of unions, so it’s important for everyone to understand, and this is such a diverse crowd looking around. I’m just proud to be able to be part of this movement to be able to be a voice for Indigenous workers,” said Sharon Giroux, the equity vice president for Indigenous workers.
Angelo Tocco, the vice president of Workers with Disabilities, Canadian Labour Congress, added, “We are fighting for equality, we are fighting for human rights, and I don’t want to speak for everyone, but I think just our presence here speaks volumes.”
Delegates will also prepare to choose the Canadian Labour Congress’s next leadership team. After four days of debate, discussion, and demonstrations, delegates now turn their attention to the future of Canada’s labour movement.
“A lot of people feel isolated now, and people feel divided. This movement is about saying no, we all need to work together. We all share something in common that’s living in a great country with great opportunities, and the richest of the rich can’t tell us that we can’t do better. We can hope for better, and we should hold together for better,” said René Jansen in de Wal, the president of the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association.
Toth added, “This is a way, in many ways, for union members to see that there’s more to just their own union in this country.”

CAPTION_ENDORSE: Protesters demand accountability following June ICE operation that resulted in nearly 50 arrests in Greene County, VA
MESSAGE_TEXT:
Community members on both sides address Greene County Board of Supervisors over June ICE arrests
GREENE COUNTY, Va. (WVIR) - Protesters gathered on Tuesday, July 14 to demand accountability following an ICE operation that resulted in nearly 50 arrests, while supporters of Sheriff Steve Smith defended the action as a matter of public safety.
ICE told 29 News the individuals arrested on June 23 were in the country illegally. Protesters said the operation lacked due process and racially profiled members of the Latino community.
The July 14 Greene County Board of Supervisors meeting marked the second protest in weeks. The first took place June 25, when people gathered along the Route 29 and Route 33 corridor — an area witnesses say was a location where many people were detained. Those at the meeting also recounted seeing abandoned work trucks left behind in the moments following the arrests.
Megan Battaile, founder of Resist Injustice Stand and Educate (RISE,) a local grassroots advocacy group, said her organization arranged the protest because members believe the sheriff’s office’s cooperation with ICE has made immigrant families feel less safe.
“I disagree that this is in regards to public safety. I think this is a fear tactic. I think we are racially profiling individuals. This is not new for our country,” Battaile said.
Supporters of Sheriff Smith said his office was assisting federal authorities to protect the community.
“These folks that the sheriff took out, all of them had arrest warrants. They were a part of gang activity. So, it’s not like he went out and said, ‘Hey, we’re just going to snatch you off the road,’” said CJ Jordan of the Greene County Gatekeepers.
29News does not currently have information confirming allegations of gang activity against those arrested.
In a Facebook statement posted on June 25, Sheriff Smith said his office works with ICE and other federal agencies to uphold the law, adding that is what the people of Greene County elected him to do.
Todd Sansom, chairman of the Greene County Republican Committee, said the sheriff is not acting alone in enforcement decisions.
“It’s important for people to understand that the sheriff is not making unilateral decisions on individuals in our community,” Sansom said. “ICE has people that they have reasons, arrest warrants and deportation warrants, whatever it might be. The sheriff is simply assisting them as they come through our community.”
Protesters and counter-protesters filled the Board of Supervisors meeting, with each speaker given a few minutes to address county leaders. Some shared personal accounts of how the operation has affected their lives.
“It’s even affected my teaching. Instead of asking me what correlation is, my students are asking me what to do if they get home and their parents are gone,” said one Greene County educator.
Others like Doug Ollivant, a Republican running for Congress in Virginia’s 7th District, voiced support for the sheriff and federal coordination.
“I support Sheriff Smith. I support ICE as a federal law enforcement agency,” Ollivant said. “It’s part of the rule of law. We are a nation of laws, lived by the rule of law. Local law enforcement should coordinate routinely with federal law enforcement.”
In a statement to 29News following the operation, ICE spokesperson Jason Koontz said local law enforcement partnerships are essential to the agency’s work.
“Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest illegal aliens across the country. When politicians bar local law enforcement from working with DHS, our law enforcement officers have to have a more visible presence so that we can find and apprehend the criminals let out of jails and back into communities,” Koontz said.
After hearing from both sides, the Greene County Board of Supervisors said it does not have the legal authority to direct how the sheriff carries out his duties, because he is an elected constitutional officer. Board members said their role is to approve the county’s budget — including funding for the sheriff’s office.
29News has not received a response from Sheriff Steve Smith at this time.

CAPTION_ENDORSE: New York Governor Hochul calls on Long Island Rail Road workers to resume bargaining after five unions representing half workforce walk out of job
MESSAGE_TEXT:
The first strike for the Long Island Rail Road in three decades has caused headaches for sports fans and commuters. The walkout, after five unions representing half the workforce walked off the job, promises to disrupt the city's transportation system.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul pleaded with unions representing workers for the Long Island Rail Road , North America’s largest commuter rail system, to resume bargaining Sunday, saying the workers and hundreds of thousands of commuters stand to lose if a strike drags on.
The walkout, the first for the LIRR since a two-day strike in 1994, promises to cause headaches for sports fans planning to see the Yankees and Mets battle this weekend or to watch the Knicks’ playoff run at Madison Square Garden, which is located directly above the railroad’s Penn Station hub in Manhattan. On Thursday, Students Supporting Israel (SSI) Rutgers chapter invited a soldier from the Israeli Defense Force (IDF) to speak in person as part of their "Triggered: From Combat to Campus" tour, while a protest against IDF presence on campus took place outside.

The event took place on the fourth floor lounge of the College Avenue Student Center at 5 p.m.
The event was met with significant criticism from groups like the Students for Justice in Palestine at New Brunswick (SJP) and the Muslim Public Relations Council (MPRC). Kelly Shapiro, co-president of SSI, opened the event by encouraging attendees to engage in open dialogue with one another. "While there may be differences of opinions among those in the space, we ask that you allow the program to proceed as planned and not interrupt the speaker," she said.
Shapiro then introduced Hertz and described his history with SSI. Hertz had been the student president of Hillel at SUNY Rockland Community College and founded the SSI chapter there, according to Shapiro.
Hertz was drafted into the IDF last year, serving in Gaza during the October 2025 ceasefire deal, said Shapiro. After being released from service two months ago, he now works as the director of Campus Affairs for the #EndJewHatred campaign.
Hertz claimed that while he was uninterested in the IDF when he was younger, he came to the conclusion as he repeatedly visited Israel himself, that his identity was tied inextricably to the area. He attempted to draft when he was 27, but said that he was denied because he was "too old" and only accepted later when Israel opened additional draft classes in response to the events of Oct. 7, 2023.
"What I'm trying to reinforce here over and over again is that the fundamental elements of Zionism (are) crucial to Jewish identity," Hertz said.

The disruptor spoke of Hind Rijab, a six-year-old from Palestine who was shot and killed by IDF soldiers firing a total of 335 bullets at her family's car in January 2024.
"When my Jewish grandmother told me about the Holocaust, she told me 'Never again,'" the disruptor said, before being ushered out of the room. "If justice is real, then the IDF will go down. You guys will be prosecuted at the Hague … Justice will prevail."
Two minutes after the first disruptor had cleared out, a second unnamed attendee began speaking back-and-forth with Hertz about death totals in Gaza. The attendee posed the statistic to Hertz of "20,000 children" killed, to which Hertz replied asking how many of them were combatants and discussed the semantics of labelling 16-year-old soldiers as "children."
Hertz responded to both disruptions by clarifying that he does not believe his government nor the IDF is perfect, but that the issue requires nuance on both sides. He commended the attendees of the talk for hearing his story and said he was "glad" the second disruptor had come to discuss things with him.
External protests before, after event
Prior to the event, the SJP organization arranged a petition in protest titled "IDF Off Our Campus: Demand that Rutgers Cancel the 'SSI Triggered' Event," partnering with organizations like the MPRC to attempt to cancel SSI's talk. As of Thursday, the petition had received more than 6,700 signatures and stood just more than halfway to its goal of 12,800.
The petition alleged that the University's permittance of IDF soldiers on campus "legitimizes all forms of Zionist violence" and neglects to acknowledge students affected by the crisis in Palestine. Additional organizations sharing the petition and campaign included NJ Build Up Resistance Now, the Arab Cultural Club, ROOTS Palestinian Cultural Club and New Jersey For Palestine alongside others.
Shapiro commented on the petition, believing it meant that Jewish students at Rutgers were being held to a double standard and silenced. "Everyday life for (Jewish students) is a difficult feat here because they're constantly being bombarded with unnecessary hate," she said. "I think … leading with love and compassion and empathy and authenticity is really our goal."
The MPRC also hosted an "IOF OFF CAMPUS" protest occurring at the College Avenue Gym at the same time as the IDF event, whose chants of "Free Palestine" could be heard from the College Avenue Student's Center's fourth floor and persisted for the latter half of the event.
Hertz referred to the chanting outside as antisemitism or "Jew hatred." He pointed to the Greek Orthodox Church and other organizations that have self-determination as a factor behind them, questioning why it was agreed upon that "Greece is for Greeks" yet felt that the same sentiment did not apply to Jewish individuals.
"(The SSI) are students who feel very strongly about their Jewish identity and their Zionism as a fundamental part of who they are as Jews," Hertz said when briefly speaking to The Daily Targum before being escorted out. "They believe that they, as Jews, have the right to self-determination, just like any group in the world, and that includes Palestinian Arabs as well."

CAPTION_ENDORSE: Union representing Oregon Trail Electric workers issues 30-day strike notice to cooperative in Baker City, OR
MESSAGE_TEXT:
Union representing Oregon Trail Electric workers issues strike notice to cooperative
Published 9:04 am Tuesday, June 23, 2026
BAKER CITY — The union that represents about 40 employees from Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative, including journeyman linemen, on Monday, June 22, issued a 30-day strike notice to the Baker City-based co-op.
The union’s goal is to negotiate a new contract with OTEC, said Nick Simons, a lineman from La Grande who was among several union members who posted signs outside OTEC’s headquarters in Baker City on Tuesday morning, June 23.
The employees, who include substation technicians, meter readers and member service representatives, are members of the International Brotherhood of Electric Workers Local 125, based in Portland.
Simons, who has worked for OTEC for more than three years, said Local 125 represents employees from cooperatives and other utilities across Oregon.
Simons, who is the La Grande delegate for the union’s negotiating team, said members of Local 125 have never gone on strike.
“We don’t want to be the first,” Simons said Tuesday morning. “We will continue to negotiate. Hopefully we can come to an agreement. All we’re asking for is a fair contract.”
The Baker City Herald has emailed OTEC asking for a comment.
Simons said the union’s current contract expired April 1 of this year. It contains a provision that the contract’s terms will continue until a new agreement is reached, he said.
Simons said the union can’t strike during the 30-day period that started with the notice to OTEC on Monday.
Union members rejected by a 34-3 vote OTEC’s most recent contract offer in early May, Simons said.
The main issue is wages, he said.
Simons said the union is asking for salary increases of 5% for the first year of a three-year deal, with 6% increases in each of the two subsequent years.
He said two other member-owned cooperatives in Oregon recently approved contracts with IBEW members that include wage hikes of about 19% over three years.
Union members who work for OTEC have been at or near the bottom of the wage scale, for IBEW members, Simons said. The union’s goal is to be between the bottom one-third to average.
“We’re OK with that,” he said. “We understand we’re in a rural community. But we feel we’re worth more.”

MESSAGE_TEXT:
SOUTH LAKE TAHOE, Calif. – The Tahoe Resistance Alliance will be holding a weekend full of activities as part of the “Good Trouble Lives On Weekend of Action” July 17-19. Events will be taking place across the country (see more here).
They will be holding peaceful events for what they say is a current threat to democracy and to protest the current state of politics in Washington, because “this is not politics as usual.”
“This is a fight for the survival of our democracy,: said local organizer Amy Machin-Ward. “Across the country, voting rights are being attacked, voices are being silenced, and the foundations of our republic are being tested. The ballot box is where the promise of America lives. If that promise is weakened, then the light of democracy grows dimmer for all of us. Inspired by the legacy of John Lewis, we choose ‘good trouble’. We choose courage over fear, action over silence, and hope over surrender.”
The Democracy is Brewing event on Friday, July 17, at Three Pines Coffee from 8 a.m. to 10 a.m. and at Paddle House Brews from 4 to 6 pm are designed to be a social and networking opportunity for individuals and organizations who share our belief in this cause. You can sign up to join the Visibility Brigade for the Rally and help them brainstorm “good trouble” actions beyond the weekend. They are planning to make this a standing gathering each month!!
The GTLO Rally at Lakeview on Saturday, July 18, from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. will provide folks an opportunity to get into some “Good Trouble” while protesting. There will be a voting status check and an online registration booth sponsored by the Young Democrats Committee at LTCC. There will be several activities for people to engage their passionate side while respecting the non-violent requirements for the Good Trouble Lives On Movement. Activities will include: Sidewalk chalk protest art, sand resistance art, human-formed messages, Resistance Music and good old-fashioned protesting on both sides of Highway 50. A Safety Team will be in place to maintain a peaceful environment for all. Attendees are encouraged to take photos of these activities and submit them to us at 5050tahoe@gmail.com for publication in our first monthly Bulletin coming out on August 1st. To RSVP to this event, please use this link:
On Sunday, July 19th – several faith-based gatherings within the Basin will be utilizing the Good Trouble Lives On “PREACH” guidelines to inform, educate and inspire their congregations with a non-partisan message about the importance of protecting the right to vote for everyone, the morality of resisting a government that threatens our civil rights, and the need to register every eligible voter possible to give the voice of the people back to them. Unity at the Lake of South Lake Tahoe is planning a service at 10:00 am.
Organizers said their goal is clear: to stand together, raise our voices responsibly, and demonstrate that the Tahoe Basin community supports democracy, accountability, and civic participation.
Commitment to Non-violence:
- This is a peaceful demonstration.
- We expect all participants to act lawfully and respectfully.
- We do not engage in or condone violence, property destruction, or confrontation.
- Participants are expected to de-escalate conflict and maintain a safe environment for families and community members.
- Weapons of any kind are not permitted.
- We are gathering to uplift democratic values — not to create harm or division.

CAPTION_ENDORSE: Parents and community advocates demand school board drop lawsuit challenging state’s new oversight board and redirect taxpayer money toward students in Memphis, TN
MESSAGE_TEXT:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. - Days after Tennessee released its final forensic audit of Memphis-Shelby County Schools (MSCS), parents and community advocates gathered Friday to demand the school board drop its lawsuit challenging the state’s new oversight board and redirect taxpayer money toward students.
The rally, organized by The Memphis Lift, came after the state audit identified more than $119 million in questioned costs tied to potential fraud, waste, abuse, and policy violations.
“I watched this baby grow up. Now she has kids in school, and her baby can’t even read. So we mad as [bleep] right now,” said Sara Carpenter, director of The Memphis Lift.
Advocates said they believe money being spent on litigation should instead support classrooms, reading intervention, special education services, and other student needs.
One parent, Dominique, said her seventh-grade son continues to struggle academically despite having an Individualized Education Program (IEP).
“My baby is in the seventh grade, and his reading level is low. They got him on a first-grade reading level,” Dominique said.
Dominique said she does not believe her son is receiving the support outlined in his IEP. Organizers said concerns like hers have prompted some parents to discuss the possibility of filing a class-action lawsuit over alleged failures to comply with students’ IEPs.
The group also referenced previous comments from former Superintendent Dr. Marie Feagins acknowledging the district had not consistently followed some students’ IEPs.
Advocates are also calling on the Memphis-Shelby County School Board to withdraw its legal challenge to Tennessee’s newly created state oversight board. Organizers estimate Shelby County has committed approximately $200,000 toward the litigation and argue those public funds would be better spent supporting students.
“We cannot steal from our children because that’s the future of Memphis,” community advocate Marcus Randolph said.
Community advocate J. Worth also criticized the district’s decision to continue the lawsuit.
“If you didn’t want the disruption, you should have stopped the corruption,” Worth said.
MSCS Superintendent Dr. Roderick Richmond said the district is taking the forensic audit seriously but believes it is important to provide additional context.
According to Richmond, the audit examined district operations from July 2021 through June 2024, a period during which MSCS managed nearly $6 billion in public funding.
Richmond said many of the issues identified in the report had already been discovered through the district’s own internal reviews before the audit was completed.
“Public discussion should always reflect the full context of the report, recognizing both the areas identified for improvement and the substantial work already underway to strengthen our district,” Richmond said. “Our response would not be driven by politics. It would be driven by students.”
Richmond also said the district has spent the past year strengthening procurement practices, financial oversight, and internal controls while continuing to focus on student achievement.
The community said accountability must continue.
Despite those assurances, community advocates said they believe elected officials should be held accountable for how taxpayer dollars are spent.
“If us citizens go out and misuse government money, we’re held accountable,” said Dianiechia Fields, director of operations for The Memphis Lift. “Right now, our elected leaders are not being held accountable.”
Advocates said they plan to continue attending school board meetings and pressing district leaders for what they believe is greater accountability.
Meanwhile, Richmond said MSCS will continue reviewing the audit’s recommendations while expanding efforts to improve transparency, strengthen operations, and prepare for the upcoming school year.

CAPTION_ENDORSE: Labor protests at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston, MA
MESSAGE_TEXT:
Thousands of nurses and home-care clinicians walked off the job Wednesday in Massachusetts, launching what their union says is the largest nurse and healthcare professional strike in state history and putting new pressure on one of the state’s most powerful hospital systems.
The strike involves more than 4,000 registered nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston and about 450 clinicians with Mass General Brigham Home Care. The Massachusetts Nurses Association called a one-day strike at Brigham beginning at 7 a.m. Wednesday, July 8. Because the hospital contracted with replacement nurses who require five-day minimum assignments, union nurses are not expected to return until 7 a.m. Monday, July 13. Home-care clinicians began a separate seven-day strike that Mass General Brigham says is scheduled to run from 8 a.m. July 8 through 7:59 a.m. July 15.
The walkout follows months of negotiations over wages, health insurance costs, working conditions, and patient-care protections. Nurses and clinicians say Mass General Brigham has refused to offer pay increases that match the cost of living in Massachusetts, while also resisting proposals they say would retain experienced staff and protect patients. Mass General Brigham says its hospitals and home-care services remain prepared to deliver safe care during the stoppage.
The strike places a labor dispute inside a larger fight over corporate healthcare power. Mass General Brigham is the largest healthcare system in Massachusetts, with flagship hospitals, community facilities, specialty services, and one of the largest hospital-based research operations in the country. The system says it is home to five nationally recognized hospitals and nearly $2 billion in annual research funding. Workers say that scale makes management’s bargaining position harder to justify.
At Brigham and Women’s, nurses say the central issue is not only wages, but whether the hospital can keep experienced bedside nurses in a region where housing, childcare, groceries, and health costs continue to rise. WBUR reported that the hospital planned to bring in more than 1,200 traveling nurses before the strike, while Boston.com reported that thousands of nurses were picketing outside the hospital Wednesday with signs reading “Boston Strikes” and “Nurses do the Labor, MGB gave No Delivery.”
The hospital has told patients it remains open. Brigham and Women’s said it has comprehensive emergency preparedness plans, including temporary nurses who will be integrated with care teams during the five-day work stoppage. The hospital said its main campus and ambulatory locations would be affected, though care and operations would mostly continue as normal. Patients were advised to keep scheduled appointments unless contacted by their care team and to allow extra travel time because of picketing and traffic near the campus.
Mass General Brigham Home Care issued similar assurances. The system said temporary licensed and credentialed clinicians had been brought in to help support patients and maintain continuity of care. It also said leaders would coordinate with referring providers to triage patients so the most acute needs would continue to be met. Some ancillary services, including dietician and speech-language therapy appointments, would be paused during the strike period.
Those contingency plans are part of management’s argument that patient care will be protected. But the union says the need for temporary workers points to a deeper failure to invest in permanent staff. Brigham nurses and home-care clinicians argue that the system is choosing short-term replacement staffing rather than reaching agreements that could stabilize the workforce.
The dispute has also drawn attention because the Brigham nurses’ strike lasts one day, while the effective work stoppage lasts five days due to the hospital’s temporary nurse contracts. The union describes that as a lockout imposed by Mass General Brigham. The hospital says the longer period is needed to meet contract requirements for replacement staff and to maintain continuity once temporary nurses are brought in.
That distinction matters politically. For workers, the lockout increases the financial penalty for striking and may chill future labor action. For the hospital, the extended work stoppage is framed as an operational necessity. For patients, the result is the same: care is being delivered during a major labor conflict involving one of the state’s most important hospitals and hundreds of home-care clinicians.
Home care is a particularly sensitive part of the dispute. Home-care clinicians serve patients outside hospital walls, including people recovering from surgery, people managing chronic illness, older adults, and patients who need skilled nursing, physical therapy, occupational therapy, case management, social work, speech therapy, nutrition services, or home health aides. When those workers strike, the impact is dispersed across homes and communities rather than concentrated at a single picket line.
Mass General Brigham says it has plans in place to support those patients. The union says the strike was forced by management’s refusal to move on fair contract terms. In a July 6 statement, MNA said both Brigham nurses and MGB Home Care clinicians had held final scheduled bargaining sessions the previous week, made significant efforts to compromise, and offered to continue negotiating to avoid a strike. The union said MGB declined opportunities to keep bargaining and refused to improve its proposals.
The wage fight is unfolding in a state where healthcare workers face the same affordability pressures as their patients. Union leaders say nurses and clinicians cannot stay in bedside and home-care roles if pay does not keep pace with local costs. They also argue that high insurance costs and reliance on temporary staff undermine retention, making it harder to maintain safe staffing and continuity of care.
Mass General Brigham has tried to reassure patients and the public that the strike will not compromise care. Brigham and Women’s said it respects and values its nurses and remains committed to a fair and responsible agreement. Home Care leaders said temporary clinicians have received training on the system’s policies, clinical protocols, systems, and expectations for patient care.
But the strike shows how far apart the two sides remain. The union is presenting the walkout as a fight over whether a wealthy hospital system will invest in permanent frontline workers. Management is presenting its response as a safe and responsible plan to keep services running while negotiations continue. Between those positions are patients, families, and clinicians navigating a healthcare system already strained by staffing shortages, high costs, and consolidation.
The next test is whether the strike brings the parties back to the table with enough movement to settle both contracts. The Brigham nurses are scheduled to return Monday morning, while the home-care strike is set to continue until Wednesday, July 15. If no agreement follows, the dispute may become a model for other healthcare workers confronting large hospital systems over wages, safety, and control of patient care.
For now, Massachusetts patients are being told care will continue while workers argue that the current model is already failing them. The union’s message to Mass General Brigham’s board was blunt: “Your decision is not based on financial necessity. It is a choice.”

MESSAGE_TEXT:
Students spilled out of class on Friday and into a May Day rally, raising their voices over housing, transportation, and student-life concerns while casting Purdue as part of a larger struggle over labor, public resources, and university accountability.
The rally, organized by Sunrise Purdue, Young Democratic Socialists of America Purdue, and other student organizers, brought students together on Memorial Mall to mark International Workers' Day.
"We're here to talk about student power and to show what student power looks like," said Raisa Deotale, a senior studying political science and co-chair of YDSA Purdue. "Walking out of campus, we're showing the administration that there is no university without the students."
Tavish Bryan, a teacher at the Kokomo Excel Center and a member of Students for a Democratic Society, said the protest was about honoring workers past and present.
"It's International Workers' Day," Bryan said. "It's a historic day for all workers, for all working people. It started in Chicago with the fight for an eight-hour workday. And we want to give respect to the martyrs who died to make this day happen,��and give respect to all workers."
But the rally's message quickly moved from labor history to Purdue-specific demands.
Organizers want Purdue to redirect more money toward students, naming transportation, housing, health care, cultural centers, and food access as priorities, said Deotale. She pointed to Purdue's financial position and said students are not seeing enough benefit from the university's resources.
"We know they have had millions of dollars of surplus in wealth, and that money is not going back to its students," Deotale said. "We want to show that when students unite, we can hold the administration accountable."
Purdue announced in August that its main campus finished fiscal year 2025 with a 4.7% positive operating margin. The university also said it had allocated $1.5 billion to capital projects, including $657 million for student success efforts. Organizers, however, argued that students are still facing basic quality-of-life problems.
Sanshray Kukulta, a political science student and coordinator of Sunrise Purdue, said Sunrise and YDSA worked together because their campaigns overlap.

Rainbow flags, trans flags, dyed hair, collapsible hand fans of every hue: Seattle’s gray skies Sunday only magnified the panoply of colors streaming up Fourth Avenue for the annual Pride Parade.
Expected to draw nearly 300,000 people, with the theme of “Rally,” this year’s parade comes to a city already bursting with visitors for the ongoing 2026 World Cup soccer matches.
And it comes amid a backlash from segments of the nation opposed to LGBTQ+ causes, and under a presidential administration that has worked to ban transgender people from military service, removed the Pride flag from Stonewall National Monument and moved to restrict gender-affirming care.
That national climate was on the mind of state Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, shortly before the event began as he stood near a parade review stand with campaign aides.
Beneath his campaign shirt, Pedersen wore a “Vote Love” T-shirt from Washington’s successful effort more than a decade ago to legalize gay marriage. He mentioned the national efforts to roll back LGBTQ+ rights, as well as two initiatives on the Washington ballot this November that he characterized as “antitrans.”
“We’re in such a crazy time in the country,” said Pedersen, adding: “So Pride is really a time for us to lock elbows collectively and insist that we’re going to continue to be a community that welcomes everyone.”
Many others had politics in mind. As the preparade entertainment in Westlake Park wound down and the marchers prepared to go forth, DonnaTella Howe, one of the parade announcers, made an oblique reference to the botched rehab of Washington, D.C.’s reflecting pool.
"It is rally, it is a party and a protest, we have a lot more to do,” said Howe. “We got to turn the reflecting pool back to blue, we got to turn more states back to blue.”
Minutes later, the parade kicked off with a swarm of bikers, their Ducatis and Hondas flying Pride flags, and leather vests and bike chassis showing off slogans with expletives against Nazis and federal immigration agents.
Not far behind the bikes were this year's grand marshals: queer activist DeAunt’e Damper and members of the Seattle Torrent women's hockey team.
Then came the floats. Alaska Airlines paraded a mock airplane, Starbucks did the same with oversized coffee cups. A University of Washington contingent decked out in Huskies gear came complete with a motorized football helmet that wheeled back and forth. People wore rainbow crowns bedecked in QFC and Fred Meyer logos.
People sat and stood shoulder to shoulder several deep along Fourth Avenue’s curbs and sidewalks. Some, like Audrey Paitz, saw their first Seattle Pride march.
“It’s just wonderful to see everybody celebrate who they are,” said Paitz, 28, of Seattle.
One new addition to this year’s parade enabled paradegoers to vote for their favorite marching contingents in three different categories, according to a news release by Seattle Pride. The categories included best float, best performance and best rally, with votes being cast on Sunday at Seattle Pride’s website.
The theme of "Rally" was chosen because it “speaks exactly to the power of showing up for one another, of making space for every voice, and of celebrating the joy and resilience that defines us,” said Patti Hearn, executive director of Seattle Pride, in that release.
There had been no disturbances or arrests along the parade route as of 3 p.m., the estimated end of the event, according to a spokesperson for Seattle's Joint Information Center.
This year’s event also saw something new: a Pride float from the first Asian country to legalize same-sex marriage.
Sponsored by the Taiwan Tourism Administration, the float featured a rainbow replica of the skyscraper known as Taipei 101, “symbolizing the bond of freedom between Seattle and Taiwan,” according to a news release by the administration.
Paris Wright, 24, had stepped out of her work on Fourth Avenue and watched the parade as the Taiwan float passed by. With everything going on politically in the nation, Wright said, Seattle’s parade is proof that “we’re not going anywhere.”
She stood near a set of oversized display photos on the sidewalk showing Seattle street scenes over the years, including one showing a 1977 gay rights parade.
Wright added: “It shows that we’re not going to back down in the face of hatred.”
